claim_text: In this dataset, the observed abnormally low ionic conductivity (σ) of the studied Li–Mn chloride spinel samples is attributed to a combination of insufficient Li-vacancy concentration (y → 0), vacancy clustering/ordering of Li and Mn on octahedral sites, and microstructure effects (grain boundaries or residual LiCl/MnCl2) that increase resistance.
Vacancy clustering and ordering of Li and Mn on octahedral sites in Li2MCl4-type spinel materials increases ionic resistance by disrupting Li-ion migration pathways.
Grain boundaries and residual secondary phases such as LiCl or MnCl2 in polycrystalline Li2MCl4 spinel solid electrolytes increase resistance and reduce bulk ionic conductivity.
Aliovalent substitution of the transition-metal site with lower-valent trivalent cations (e.g., V3+ or Sc3+) produces Li deficiencies (Li vacancies) via charge compensation.
Quench cooling from high temperature can freeze high-temperature disorder (suppress ordering), whereas slow cooling can allow ordering to develop in crystalline solids.

Low-angle superlattice reflections observed by synchrotron X-ray diffraction can be used to detect long-range ordering in these materials, and neutron diffraction can be used to confirm site occupancies (e.g., Li vs transition-metal occupations).

Pellet processing parameters (e.g., applied pressure, dwell time, and sintering temperature) influence microstructure (such as grain boundary density) and thereby affect the measured bulk ionic conduction in solid electrolyte pellets.
In Li2MCl4-type spinel systems, tetravalent (4+) dopants (for example Zr4+) can drive stronger octahedral ordering and/or produce Li2ZrCl6-type impurity phases.
Within this experimental campaign, V3+-doped samples were previously synthesized as single-phase spinel when processed at 400 °C.
A synthesis temperature of 400 °C reduces volatility of ZrCl4 relative to higher temperatures, helping to limit ZrCl4 loss during solid-state synthesis of Zr-containing chloride spinels.
Li2MnCl4 synthesized at 400 °C is single-phase spinel according to X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis.
Li2MnCl4 synthesized at 400 °C exhibits an ionic conductivity of 8.81e-07 S/cm.

The ionic conductivity of Li2MnCl4 synthesized at 400 °C (8.81e-07 S/cm) is 1–2 orders of magnitude lower than Li-vacancy-rich analogs measured in this dataset, for example Li1.6Mn0.9V0.2Cl4 (2.04e-05 S/cm), Li1.4Mn0.8Ta0.2Cl4 (2.15e-05 S/cm), and Sc-doped samples (4.63e-05–6.43e-05 S/cm).
Even relative to other nominally stoichiometric or lightly doped compositions in this experimental campaign, the 8.81e-07 S/cm conductivity for Li2MnCl4 at 400 °C is anomalously low.

The XRD pattern of the 400 °C Li2MnCl4 sample shows notable unindexed features, including a strong missing peak at approximately 30.46° 2θ, suggesting subtle deviations from the ideal Fd-3m spinel model (possible weak ordering or slight symmetry lowering).
A second Li2MnCl4 sample synthesized at 350 °C contains major MnCl2 and LiCl impurities by XRD and exhibits an even lower ionic conductivity of 3.77e-07 S/cm.

In this dataset, microstructure and impurity effects (as observed in the 350 °C Li2MnCl4 sample with MnCl2/LiCl impurities) can further suppress ionic conduction, as evidenced by the lower measured conductivity.

Within the context of these experiments, stoichiometric Li content in Li2MnCl4 likely results in too few mobile Li vacancies and promotes Li/M octahedral ordering, both of which are asserted to increase Li-ion migration barriers.

In this campaign's samples, low-temperature synthesis at 400 °C combined with the presence of highly charged Nb5+ drives strong octahedral-site ordering and Li-vacancy ordering (e.g., Imma/Cmmm-type cation order) that blocks the 16d–48f–16c Li-percolation network, yielding a locally ordered, Li-vacancy–trapped state with extremely poor Li mobility.

Minor, possibly nanoscale, Nb–Cl–rich grain-boundary phases that are below XRD detection or poorly fit in Rietveld analysis may be present in these samples and may further increase grain-boundary resistance.
The octahedral ionic radius of Mn2+ is larger than that of Fe2+ (r_oct(Mn2+) > r_oct(Fe2+)), so substituting Mn2+ for Fe2+ in spinel structures introduces size and field-strength disorder.
Size/field-strength disorder in spinel compounds is known to suppress long-range cation ordering.
In Li-containing chloride spinels, weakening of Nb–vacancy associations (e.g., via cation-site disorder) can reopen Li-ion migration pathways, increasing Li mobility.
Niobium chloride (NbClx) species are volatile at elevated temperatures, so synthesis at lower temperatures (around 450 °C) is used to limit NbClx volatility.
Mn/Nb-containing spinel chloride materials have been observed under similar synthesis conditions to exhibit room-temperature ionic conductivities on the order of 1e-5 to 1e-6 S/cm.
This sample is indexed as spinel (Fd-3m) at greater than 96% phase fraction according to its XRD analysis.
This sample exhibits an ultralow room-temperature ionic conductivity of 1.0e-12 S/cm.

Within this dataset, vacancy-rich inverse spinels with similar lithium deficiency (y ≈ 0.6) and comparable synthesis temperatures show room-temperature conductivities clustering around 1e-6–1e-5 S/cm (examples are Fe-, Mn-, and Mg-based Nb/Ta-doped spinels in the campaign).

Direct peer compositions in the dataset have the following room-temperature ionic conductivities: Li1.4Mn0.8Nb0.2Cl4 = 8.36e-06 S/cm; Li1.4Mg0.8Nb0.2Cl4 = 5.81e-06 S/cm; Li2FeCl4 = 1.14e-05 S/cm; Li1.4Fe0.8Ta0.2Cl4 = 4.57e-05 S/cm.
The sample's conductivity (1.0e-12 S/cm) is lower than the cited peer conductivities by approximately 6–7 orders of magnitude (comparing ~1e-6–1e-5 S/cm peers to 1e-12 S/cm).
The sample's X-ray diffraction pattern shows a strong extra low-angle peak near 14.94° 2θ.
Low-angle extra peaks in XRD (such as a peak near 14.94° 2θ) are consistent with cation/vacancy-ordering superstructure reflections that may not be captured by an average 'Fd-3m' spinel match.
Cation/vacancy ordering (i.e., an ordered variant of a spinel) can severely suppress lithium-ion migration even when the average diffraction symmetry appears spinel-like.

In Cr-containing Li2MCl4 spinel samples from this dataset, Cr3+ induces strong octahedral-site ordering and Li-vacancy ordering consistent with local Imma/Cmmm derivative structures, and forms defect associates (Cr_M^•–V_Li′ pairs) that immobilize Li vacancies.

In these samples, minor Li2CrCl4-like and/or poorly crystalline intergranular phases increase grain-boundary resistance and reduce the measured ionic conductivity down to the instrument detection floor.
Cr3+ in chloride spinel environments strongly prefers octahedral coordination (i.e., Cr3+ is strongly octahedral) in Li2MCl4-type spinels.
In Li1.5Mg0.5Cr0.5Cl4, Li-vacancy and cation ordering and defect association are likely to immobilize lithium ions, reducing Li mobility in that composition.
A lithium vacancy concentration of y = 0.2 (20% vacancies) provides a sufficient vacancy fraction for percolation of Li transport in Li2MCl4-type spinels.
The synthesis temperature of 450 °C has been used historically for Li–Mg–Cl spinels (for example, historical syntheses of Li2MgCl4).
Synthesis at 450 °C for Li–Mg–Cl spinels tends to complete the solid-state reaction without significant chloride loss and tends to yield higher phase purity compared to synthesis at 400 °C.

Reducing the fraction of strongly octahedral Cr3+ in Li2MCl4-type compositions is expected to weaken the driving force for formation of ordered Imma/Cmmm derivative structures and to reduce the propensity for Li2CrCl4-like impurity phases.
This sample was assigned 93.5% to the spinel phase (space group Fd-3m) and exhibits an ionic conductivity of 1.0e-12 S/cm.

The sample's conductivity (1.0e-12 S/cm) is orders of magnitude lower than conductivities measured in this dataset for Li2MgCl4 (4.2e-06 to 2.91e-06 S/cm), Li1.5Mn0.5Cr0.5Cl4 (6.76e-08 S/cm), and Li1.5Mg0.5V0.5Cl4 (3.01e-07 S/cm).

Refinement of this sample produced an unusually high Rwp and extra or missing diffraction peaks, which suggests structural heterogeneity and possible cation/vacancy ordering not captured by the automated 'spinel' phase label.
Cr3+ exhibits a strong preference for octahedral coordination (octahedral site preference).
In inverse spinel structures, extensive lithium-vacancy ordering and defect association are known to suppress Li-ion mobility.

In the lithium chloride spinel samples studied here, incorporation of Cr3+ induces strong octahedral-site ordering and Li-vacancy ordering, yielding local structures corresponding to Imma/Cmmm derivative symmetries.
Cr3+ in the studied spinel compositions forms defect associates (Cr_M^•–V_Li′ pairs) that immobilize Li vacancies.

Minor Li2CrCl4-like and/or poorly crystalline intergranular phases present in the samples increase grain-boundary resistance and drive the measured ionic conductivity down to the instrument detection floor.
This sample was assigned 93.5% to the spinel (Fd-3m) phase.
This sample shows a near-insulating ionic conductivity of 1.0e-12 S/cm.
The sample's conductivity (1.0e-12 S/cm) is orders of magnitude lower than Mg- and Cr-containing peer samples in this dataset.
Li2MgCl4 measured in this dataset has a conductivity in the range 4.2e-06 to 2.91e-06 S/cm.
Li1.5Mn0.5Cr0.5Cl4 measured in this dataset has a conductivity of 6.76e-08 S/cm.
The heavily two-phase Li1.5Mg0.5V0.5Cl4 measured in this dataset has a conductivity of 3.01e-07 S/cm.

The diffraction data for this sample show an unusually high Rwp and extra/missing peaks, which suggest structural heterogeneity and possible cation/vacancy ordering not captured by the automated 'spinel' phase label.
Cr3+ has a strong octahedral site preference.
Li-vacancy ordering and defect association are known to suppress Li mobility in inverse spinels.
Given the strong octahedral preference of Cr3+, extensive Li-vacancy ordering and defect association are likely in this specific sample.
In solid-state reactions conducted at 450 °C, Zn2+ disrupts the inverse spinel stability field and favors formation of non-spinel Li2ZnCl4-like and separate MCl2 phases.
A phase assemblage consisting of non-spinel Li2ZnCl4-like and MCl2 phases precludes the vacancy/disorder required for Li+ transport in Li2MCl4-type spinels and yields negligible ionic conductivity.
Aliovalent co-doping in Li2MCl4 spinel compositions induces Li vacancies via charge compensation and can be used to stabilize the spinel (Fd-3m) framework by creating vacancy disorder.
High-energy mechanochemical pre-milling prior to heating promotes more homogeneous cation distribution and can suppress cation segregation during subsequent solid-state synthesis of chloride spinels.
Historical data from this dataset show that Co/Mg and Co/Mn 50:50 solid solutions synthesized at 450 °C form single-phase spinel and exhibit ionic conductivities on the order of 10^-6–10^-5 S/cm.
Historical data from this dataset show that the 50% Zn sample decomposed into LiCl and CoCl2 and exhibited negligible ionic conductivity.
Zn2+ has a propensity for tetrahedral coordination that can destabilize the spinel network in chloride-based spinel systems.
ZnCl2 melts below 450 °C (and therefore is molten at 450 °C), and molten ZnCl2 can act to promote phase segregation during high-temperature synthesis.

The Zn-containing composition in this series (unlike analogous 50–50 M-site mixtures such as Li2Co0.5Mg0.5Cl4 and Li2Co0.5Mn0.5Cl4) fails to form any inverse spinel and instead is a mixture of LiCl and CoCl2.
The Zn-containing composition described above exhibits an insulating ionic conductivity of 1e-12 S/cm.
Analogous 50–50 mixtures on the M site (for example, Li2Co0.5Mg0.5Cl4 and Li2Co0.5Mn0.5Cl4) form inverse spinel phases in this series.
Zn2+ has a strong structural preference and forms orthorhombic Li2ZnCl4 (space group Pnma) rather than adopting the inverse spinel framework.

Under the reported synthesis condition of 450 °C, ZnCl2 (melting point approximately 290 °C) can act as a flux and promote segregation into non-spinel Zn- and Co-chlorides rather than stabilizing the spinel framework.

At 450 °C, Zn2+ disrupts the inverse spinel stability field in Li2MCl4 compositions, favoring formation of nonspinel Li2ZnCl4-like and MCl2 phases, which precludes the vacancy/disorder needed for Li+ transport and yields a phase assemblage with negligible ionic conductivity.
Yttrium trichloride (YCl3) has a melting point of approximately 721 °C.
In Li2−yM1Cl4 inverse spinel compositions, aliovalent trivalent substitution (for example Y3+ substituting for Co2+) creates lithium vacancies via charge compensation.
Lithium vacancies in inverse spinel structures are known to enhance three-dimensional Li+ percolation (i.e., improve 3D Li+ conduction pathways).
Y3+ ions strongly prefer octahedral coordination in crystal structures (octahedral site preference for Y3+).
Within this experimental campaign, Co/Mg and Co/Mn chloride compositions formed spinel phases under synthesis conditions at about 450 °C.
The Zn-containing 50:50 M-site composition studied in this dataset failed to form any inverse spinel and was instead a mixture of LiCl and CoCl2.
The Zn-containing sample exhibited an insulating ionic conductivity of 1e-12 S/cm.
Analogous 50:50 M-site mixtures in this study, specifically Li2Co0.5Mg0.5Cl4 and Li2Co0.5Mn0.5Cl4, form inverse spinel phases (unlike the Zn-containing composition).
Zn2+ has a strong structural preference: Zn forms orthorhombic Li2ZnCl4 (Pnma) rather than the inverse spinel framework.
ZnCl2 has a melting point of approximately 290 °C.
At 450 °C, molten ZnCl2 can act as a flux and, in this study, promoted segregation into non-spinel Zn- and Co-chlorides instead of stabilizing the spinel framework.

In lithium chloride spinel (Li2MCl4) structures, lithium ions occupy a three-dimensional network of tetrahedral and octahedral sites (a tetra–octa network) that provides pathways for Li-ion migration.
Aliovalent substitution of trivalent cations (for example V3+) on the M site in Li2MCl4-type spinels produces lithium vacancies via charge compensation.
Clustering of lithium vacancies or re-establishment of cation/vacancy ordering can reduce lithium-ion mobility in solid electrolytes such as Li2MCl4 spinels.

Quenching (rapid cooling) versus slow cooling during synthesis affects the degree of cation ordering in spinel chloride materials, with quenching tending to preserve disorder and slow cooling allowing ordering to develop.

The suppression or appearance of superlattice X-ray diffraction peaks near approximately 15° 2θ in chloride spinel diffraction patterns is commonly used as an indicator of the degree of cation ordering.
7Li nuclear magnetic resonance (7Li NMR) spectroscopy can be used to detect and quantify changes in lithium mobility in solid electrolytes, including lithium halide spinels.
In this experimental campaign, spinel phase purity was achieved for the composition with x = 0.15 when synthesized at 400 °C.
A vacancy-rich spinel sample in this dataset exhibits an ionic conductivity of 2.59e-05 S/cm (measured for the sample described as vacancy-rich).
In this dataset, Li2MnCl4 samples synthesized at similar temperatures exhibited an ionic conductivity of 5.95e-06 S/cm.
In this dataset, Li2FeCl4 samples synthesized at similar temperatures exhibited an ionic conductivity of 1.14e-05 S/cm.
In this dataset, the higher-V sample Li1.5Mn0.5V0.5Cl4 (synthesized at similar temperatures) exhibited an ionic conductivity of 2.86e-06 S/cm.

Within this dataset, the V = 0.15 composition is reported to be close to an optimum that maximizes mobile Li-vacancy concentration and cation/Li disorder without tipping into vacancy clustering or cation-order-driven blocking observed at higher V levels.
The measured conductivity of 2.59e-05 S/cm for the vacancy-rich spinel is an outlier on the high side among genuine spinel samples in this dataset.
In this dataset, higher V compositions show observations of vacancy clustering or cation-order-driven blocking.

In Li2MCl4-type lithium halide spinel solid electrolytes (e.g., Li2−yFe1−xTaxCl4), substitution of Ta5+ at approximately 20% is claimed to produce an optimal lithium-vacancy concentration of y ≈ 0.6, to enhance Li/transition‑metal disorder on octahedral sites without triggering long‑range ordering, and thereby maximize connectivity of the 16d–48f–16c Li‑ion migration network.

In lithium halide spinel solid electrolytes, replacing Cl− with F− increases lattice binding energy via stronger Li–F interactions and reduces polarizability, which raises Li‑ion migration energy barriers.
In these experiments, introduction of Br− was observed (as seen in XRD) to promote formation of a secondary LiCl phase, which lowers the effective percolation of the spinel phase.

In this study, reducing Ta content from x = 0.20 to x = 0.15 (target composition Li1.55Fe0.85Ta0.15Cl4) increases the Li content to Li = 1.55 (y = 0.45), which lowers the lithium vacancy concentration and is expected to decrease the connectivity of the 16d–48f–16c Li migration network.

In prior observations/known reports for these chloride spinel systems, maintaining a pure chloride halide sublattice (no F or Br substitution) avoids conductivity-degrading effects that have been observed when F or Br are present on the halide sublattice.

Within this experimental campaign, synthesizing Li1.4Fe0.8Ta0.2Cl4 at 400 °C produced the highest ionic conductivity and resulted in minimal impurity phases compared with other tested synthesis temperatures.

In this dataset, a Ta5+-doped spinel sample synthesized at 400 °C exhibits an ionic conductivity of 4.57e-05 S/cm and this value is one of the highest conductivities observed in the dataset, exceeding those of most Fe-, Mn-, and Mg-based spinels.
Within this dataset, the composition Li1.4Mn0.8Ta0.2Cl4 was measured to have an ionic conductivity of 5.16e-06 S/cm.
Within this dataset, the composition Li1.4Co0.8Ta0.2Cl4 was measured to have an ionic conductivity of 1.97e-07 S/cm.
Within this dataset, the composition Li1.4Fe0.8Nb0.2Cl4 was measured to have an ionic conductivity of 1e-12 S/cm.
In this dataset for the same composition series, partial halide mixing with F (fluorine) reduces the ionic conductivity to 3.03e-05 S/cm compared to the Ta5+-doped chloride sample.
In this dataset for the same composition series, halide mixing with Br (bromine) leads to the formation of a LiCl impurity and further reduces the ionic conductivity to 1.52e-05 S/cm.

Based on observations in this dataset, the Ta5+-doped composition is a positive outlier among true inverse spinels, indicating a favorable defect/disorder landscape that is sensitive to both the identity of the high-valent dopant and the halide sublattice.

Ta5+ substitution at approximately 20% in Li-halide spinel compositions drives an Li-vacancy concentration of about y ≈ 0.6, enhances Li/M disorder on octahedral sites without triggering long-range ordering, and thereby maximizes connectivity of the 16d–48f–16c Li-ion migration network.
Substituting F− for Cl− in lithium halide spinel electrolytes increases lattice binding energy via stronger Li–F interactions, reduces lattice polarizability, and raises Li-ion migration barriers.
Substituting Br− in these samples promotes formation of secondary LiCl (observed by XRD in this campaign), which lowers the effective percolation of the spinel phase.
In prior experiments within this dataset, full substitution of the Fe co-host by Mn at the same Ta5+ level (x = 0.20) underperformed relative to other compositions.
Ta5+ substitution at x = 0.20 in these Li–M–Cl spinel compositions produces a favorable lithium-vacancy level (as observed in this dataset).
Mg2+ is a non-Jahn–Teller (non-JT) octahedral 2+ cation and has a smaller octahedral ionic radius than Fe2+.
Replacing Cl with F or Br in chloride spinel electrolytes has been observed to suppress ionic conductivity.
TaCl5 is volatile at elevated temperatures, so lowering synthesis temperature (e.g., to ~400 °C) reduces TaCl5 volatility while still allowing spinel-phase formation.
A Ta5+-doped spinel synthesized at 400 °C exhibits ionic conductivity of 4.57e-05 S/cm in this dataset.
The Ta5+-doped spinel conductivity (4.57e-05 S/cm) is well above the conductivities of most Fe-, Mn-, and Mg-based spinels reported in this dataset.
In this dataset, Li1.4Mn0.8Ta0.2Cl4 shows ionic conductivity of 5.16e-06 S/cm.
In this dataset, Li1.4Co0.8Ta0.2Cl4 shows ionic conductivity of 1.97e-07 S/cm.
In this dataset, Li1.4Fe0.8Nb0.2Cl4 shows ionic conductivity of 1e-12 S/cm.
In this dataset, partial substitution of F into the halide sublattice at the Ta5+-doped composition reduces ionic conductivity to 3.03e-05 S/cm (i.e., F partly suppresses σ).
In this dataset, partial substitution of Br into the halide sublattice at the Ta5+-doped composition introduces a LiCl impurity and reduces ionic conductivity to 1.52e-05 S/cm.
Within the dataset, the Ta5+-doped composition is a positive outlier among true inverse spinels in terms of ionic conductivity.

Observations in this dataset indicate the favorable defect/disorder landscape of the Ta5+-doped spinel is sensitive to both the identity of the high-valent dopant and to changes in the halide sublattice.
This study/dataset reports an unusually high ionic conductivity in some Li2−yMn1−xScxCl4 spinel samples (the hypothesis is posed to explain that unusually high conductivity).
The hypothesis asserts that a very high Li-vacancy concentration in the Li2−yMn1−xScxCl4 series (y ≈ 0.5) contributes to the unusually high ionic conductivity observed.
The hypothesis asserts that size and charge mismatch between Mn2+ and Sc3+ suppresses Li/M octahedral ordering in Li2−yMn1−xScxCl4 spinels.

The hypothesis asserts that microstructural percolation between two closely related spinel domains with slightly different lattice parameters can create a highly connected 3D network of edge- and face-sharing Li sites, which reduces migration barriers and enhances Li-ion transport in these materials.
The hypothesis states that the observed high conductivity in these materials is an intrinsic ionic effect (not electronic).
The hypothesis asserts that frustrated cation ordering in these Li2−yMn1−xScxCl4 materials remains frozen at temperatures of 400–450 °C.
Mn is referenced in the text as Mn2+ and Sc as Sc3+, i.e., the composition discussion treats manganese in the +2 oxidation state and scandium in the +3 oxidation state.
For aliovalent Sc3+ substitution on Mn2+ in Li2MCl4-type compositions, charge neutrality requires the aliovalent substitution parameter y to equal x (y = x).
The composition Li1.6Mn0.6Sc0.4Cl4 corresponds to x = y = 0.4 under the Li2-xMxScyCl4 (aliovalent substitution) notation used in this study.
Compared to the x = 0.5 composition Li1.5Mn0.5Sc0.5Cl4, Li1.6Mn0.6Sc0.4Cl4 has reduced Sc content (i.e., lower Sc fraction).
Li1.6Mn0.6Sc0.4Cl4 retains a very high lithium-vacancy fraction (vacancy-rich) despite the reduced Sc content relative to the x = 0.5 composition.
Within this experimental campaign/dataset, the x = 0.5 sample Li1.5Mn0.5Sc0.5Cl4 was identified as an 'abnormal' sample exhibiting high ionic conductivity (anomalously elevated σ).
Prior syntheses in this study used a 400 °C synthesis protocol (the 400 °C protocol is the protocol used previously in this dataset).
Synthesis at 400 °C minimizes halide volatilization (i.e., using 400 °C reduces halide loss during synthesis).
This sample (a chloride inverse spinel) shows exceptionally high room-temperature ionic conductivity of 4.63e-05 S/cm.
The room-temperature conductivity of 4.63e-05 S/cm for this chloride inverse spinel exceeds the typical 1e-6–1e-5 S/cm range observed for closely related spinel compositions in this study.
In this dataset, Li2MnCl4 was measured to have ionic conductivity of approximately 6e-06 S/cm (room temperature).
In this dataset, Li1.4Mn0.8Nb0.2Cl4 was measured to have ionic conductivity of approximately 8e-06 S/cm (room temperature).
In this dataset, Li1.6Mn0.8Zr0.2Cl4 was measured to have ionic conductivity of approximately 6e-06 S/cm (room temperature).
X-ray diffraction (XRD) refinement of this sample fits to two spinel-like references: 'spinel (Fd-3m)' with fraction 0.7726 and 'Li2MnCl4 (Fd-3m)' with fraction 0.2274.
The XRD refinement for this sample suggests two closely related spinel domains with slightly different lattice parameters rather than the presence of foreign phases.

In this dataset, isovalent Sc3+ doping on other divalent hosts produced lower room-temperature conductivities under similar conditions: Li1.5Mg0.5Sc0.5Cl4 ≈ 2.2e-06 S/cm and Li1.5Co0.5Sc0.5Cl4 ≈ 2.68e-07 S/cm.
In this dataset, Li1.5Fe0.5Sc0.5Cl4 was measured with conductivity ≈ 1.37e-05 S/cm, but that sample is nonspinel and was reported as likely electronically leaky.

The combination in the studied composition of Mn2+ (described here as large high-spin d5 with weak octahedral preference) and aliovalent Sc3+ (described here as having strong octahedral preference) at x = 0.5 implies a very high Li-vacancy content (y ≈ 0.5) and strong Li/M disorder for that composition in this dataset.

The inferred high Li-vacancy content and strong Li/M disorder for the Mn2+/Sc3+ x=0.5 composition are consistent with a conductivity jump, but the magnitude measured here (4.63e-05 S/cm) is abnormal compared with the broader series of compositions in this study.
For the composition Li1.4Mn0.8Ta0.2Cl4, a lower synthesis temperature (400 °C) yields a more disordered inverse spinel with greater Li/M octahedral disorder.
For Li1.4Mn0.8Ta0.2Cl4, synthesis at 400 °C produces a higher concentration of unassociated Li vacancies that are attributed to Ta5+ aliovalent substitution.
For Li1.4Mn0.8Ta0.2Cl4, synthesis at 450 °C drives partial cation ordering consistent with an incipient Imma/Cmmm superstructure.
In this system (Li1.4Mn0.8Ta0.2Cl4), the development of cation ordering raises the Li-ion migration barrier and lowers the ionic conductivity (σ).
Cation ordering in these spinel/chloride systems is expected to produce low-angle superlattice reflections in X-ray diffraction at approximately 15° 2θ.
Aliovalent substitution of higher-valent cations (e.g., Ta5+) in Li2MCl4-type spinels produces Li vacancies via charge compensation.
Sc3+ is typically available as ScCl3, which is a stable scandium chloride with low volatility (context: substitution uses Sc3+ as ScCl3 due to its stability and low volatility).

In this experimental campaign, synthesis at 400 °C previously produced a clean spinel phase and a higher ionic conductivity for the composition Li1.4Mn0.8Ta0.2Cl4 (context: 400 °C was chosen because it already yielded a clean spinel and higher σ for Li1.4Mn0.8Ta0.2Cl4).

Cation ordering in these lithium chloride spinel materials manifests as a low-angle superlattice reflection near approximately 15° 2θ in X-ray diffraction (context: the orthogonal test aims to frustrate cation ordering, reducing superlattice intensity near ~15° 2θ).
A sample synthesized at 400 °C indexed as spinel (space group Fd-3m, Rwp = 5.42%) and exhibited ionic conductivity σ = 2.15e-05 S/cm.
A sample synthesized at 450 °C indexed as spinel (space group Fd-3m, Rwp = 7.32%) and exhibited ionic conductivity σ = 5.16e-06 S/cm.
Within this dataset, the 400 °C sample has approximately 4× higher ionic conductivity than the 450 °C sample (2.15e-05 vs 5.16e-06 S/cm).
In this experimental campaign, syntheses at 450 °C usually produce equal or higher ionic conductivity than lower-temperature syntheses, attributed to better phase purity and densification.
The X-ray diffraction pattern of the 450 °C sample shows a stronger low-angle signal near 15° 2θ (missing-peak intensity ~0.3) than the 400 °C sample (missing-peak intensity ~0.15).
The stronger low-angle signal observed in the 450 °C pattern is consistent with greater cation ordering resulting from higher-temperature synthesis.
Cation ordering in inverse spinels is known to penalize Li+ transport.
In this dataset, samples described as Li3.66Fe2.17Cl8-rich exhibited abnormally high measured conductivity (σ) relative to expected Li+ superionic transport.
The dataset shows a reproducibility gap in the measured conductivity of these Fe-containing samples (i.e., conductivity values are not consistently reproducible across measurements/batches).

Mixed-valent Fe2+/Fe3+ centers and related Fe-containing networks (e.g., FeClx) in chloride materials can give rise to electronic conduction (electronic leakage) that can dominate the total measured conductivity and mimic or obscure true Li+ ionic transport.
Undetected nanocrystalline or amorphous Li-rich phases present within a sample can contribute to elevated measured conductivity, potentially affecting interpretation of bulk ionic transport.
A prior sample in this experimental campaign was identified as an outlier with a room-temperature conductivity (σ_RT) of 3.53e-05 S/cm.
Lithium chloride (LiCl) is highly insulating; in this study it is used as an inert buffer intended to dilute possible intergranular FeClx / mixed-valent networks.
Maintaining the same synthesis temperature of 400 °C as in prior syntheses preserves comparability and minimizes additional Fe redox changes or volatilization that can occur at other temperatures.
One sample from this dataset was refined as 76.97% Li3.66Fe2.17Cl8 (Cmmm) + 23.03% CrCl3 and exhibited an ionic conductivity of σ = 3.53e-05 S/cm.
Two other syntheses of the same nominal composition in this dataset were spinel/FeCl2-rich and had conductivities of σ = 1.58e-08 S/cm and σ = 2.17e-07 S/cm (nearly insulating).

The sample refined as 76.97% Li3.66Fe2.17Cl8 + 23.03% CrCl3 (σ = 3.53e-05 S/cm) is an extreme outlier in conductivity compared to the two other syntheses of the same nominal composition in this dataset.
The high-conductivity sample (σ = 3.53e-05 S/cm) is not a spinel phase and contains mixed-valent iron chloride phases.
Mixed-valent iron chloride phases can introduce electronic leakage (i.e., electronic conduction).
The conductivity of the non-spinel mixed-valent Fe chloride sample (σ = 3.53e-05 S/cm) is comparable to the best spinel samples in this dataset despite its non-spinel structure.
X-ray diffraction (XRD) of the high-conductivity sample does not show evidence of a hidden nanocrystalline Li-rich Sc/Y-like chloride phase.

Based on the observed phase assemblage in this dataset, the high conductivity of the non-spinel sample cannot be reconciled without invoking either electronic conduction or a hidden nanocrystalline Li-rich Sc/Y-like chloride phase.
Slight LiCl exsolution during synthesis drives the Li-cloride spinel matrix to be slightly Li-deficient, which maximizes mobile Li-vacancy concentration and increases Li/M disorder.

Octahedral cation size mismatch (e.g., among Mn, V, Nb) raises configurational disorder, which frustrates octahedral cation ordering, increases Li site energy degeneracy, and can lower Li migration barriers.

The chloride lattice is relatively soft, and mixing heavier or higher-valence cations can broaden the distribution of Li migration bottlenecks and increase the likelihood of low-barrier Li-ion migration pathways.
Absence of redox-active, mixed-valent Fe reduces the risk of electronic leakage in chloride spinel compositions compared with Fe-containing, mixed-valence materials.
The proposed composition combines two motifs that were associated with high ionic conductivity in the dataset: light V3+ substitution and a small pentavalent dopant to tune vacancy concentration.

In this dataset, Y3+ produced large conductivity signals in mixed-cation chloride spinel compositions (examples include Mn/Y and Co/Y mixed samples).

In the dataset, small additions of high-valence cations (Ta5+ or Nb5+) were observed to tune Li vacancy concentration and, when used sparingly, can increase ionic conductivity; by contrast, excessive high-valence content or high synthesis/anneal temperature in these samples was observed to drive cation ordering and lower ionic conductivity.

In the dataset, the presence of low-angle superlattice reflections in chloride spinel samples correlates with lower ionic conductivity (i.e., suppressed/absent low-angle superlattice peaks correlate with higher conductivity).

Aliovalent (trivalent or higher-valence) substitution in Li2MCl4 spinel-type materials produces Li vacancies via charge compensation (creating cation charge imbalance that is compensated by reducing Li content).
Mn2+ in octahedral coordination has an ionic radius of approximately 0.83 Å (VI coordination) and Y3+ in octahedral coordination has an ionic radius of approximately 0.90 Å (VI coordination).

Because Y3+ is larger than Mn2+, substitution of Y3+ on the octahedral cation sublattice produces local tensile strain and can increase site disorder that frustrates Li/cation ordering in spinel chloride frameworks.

Mixing multiple different cations on the same crystallographic sublattice increases configurational entropy and can suppress long-range cation ordering in crystalline solids, thereby reducing ordered superlattice reflections.
High Y content in Li–Y–Cl compositions can lead to formation/precipitation of Li3YCl6 as a separate phase in chloride syntheses.
Most high-σ spinels in this dataset cluster around Li ≈ 1.4–1.6 (i.e., compositions with lithium content near 1.4–1.6 per formula unit show the highest ionic conductivities in the dataset).

The dataset indicates that metal-rich or metal-excess variants are an underexplored lever that can change vacancy topology and potentially open alternative percolation motifs.
Small Nb5+ additions in the dataset often act as strong vacancy generators, but Nb/Ta fractions and synthesis temperature must be carefully controlled to avoid ordering.
In many Nb/Ta-containing entries in the dataset, ordering correlates with reduced ionic conductivity (σ).

Across prior samples in this dataset, Mn2+-rich host compositions consistently favored higher ionic conductivity and resisted the Li/M ordering that was observed for Ni- and Co-containing samples.
In this dataset, limiting the trivalent dopant fraction to modest values (≤ 0.15) correlated with a reduced propensity for forming secondary Li6MCl8 or other MClx impurity phases.
Dataset evidence shows that vanadium can be reduced and segregate at low synthesis temperatures: Li6VCl8 and FeCl2 impurity phases were observed in samples synthesized at 400 °C.
In samples from this study, a high Li-vacancy regime (high aliovalent dopant fraction) promoted Cmmm-type ordering in some compositions.

Aliovalent substitution of a trivalent cation (V3+) for a divalent M2+ in Li2MCl4 spinels removes one Li+ per substituted site and thereby creates Li-site vacancies that can increase mobile-site connectivity for Li-ion transport when the vacancy density is moderate.

V3+ has a smaller ionic radius than Mn2+, and such substitution is expected to introduce local octahedral distortions that promote Li/M site mixing and can flatten the Li potential-energy landscape (i.e., increase structural disorder beneficial for Li mobility).

A larger divalent host cation (Mn2+ relative to smaller divalent cations) expands tetrahedral→octahedral diffusion windows in spinel lattices, which can widen Li+ diffusion pathways (bottleneck tuning) and thereby facilitate Li-ion transport.

In this dataset, low-level trivalent substitution (~0.1) in an Fe2+ spinel host is commonly tolerated and can tune Li vacancy concentration without forcing phase separation; example: Li1.9Fe0.9In0.1Cl4 was refined as a single-phase spinel and delivered ionic conductivity in the mid-10^-6 S/cm range.
Within this experimental campaign, small trivalent dopants at approximately 0.1 formula fraction were successfully incorporated in Fe-based chloride spinels when synthesized at 450 °C.
Larger, more polarizable trivalent dopants were not systematically explored in this dataset.

In several systems observed in the dataset, incorporation of heavier, more polarizable anions/cations correlated with softer lattices and improved ionic conductivity when those species were incorporated without forming separate phases.

Bi3+ is a relatively large trivalent cation with a larger ionic radius and higher electronic polarizability (compared with In3+), properties relevant to octahedral coordination in chloride spinel lattices.

In Li halide spinel frameworks, incorporating large, highly polarizable cations on the octahedral sublattice can increase dielectric screening and reduce the Coulomb contribution to the Li+ migration barrier.

Increasing the average M–Cl bond length by substituting larger octahedral cations can slightly expand the unit cell, widen tetrahedral–octahedral bottlenecks for Li, and lower the activation energy for Li+ hops in spinel structures.
Bi3+ can exhibit limited solubility in chloride matrices and may form Bi–Cl secondary phases if over-doped or if synthesis/conditions are inappropriate.

Rietveld X‑ray/Neutron diffraction analysis can fail to detect nanoscale or amorphous minority phases, so a nanoscale Li3YCl6 phase could escape Rietveld detection in lithium chloride spinel syntheses.

Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measures total conductivity, so partial electronic conduction (for example from electronically conducting transition‑metal chlorides) can inflate the EIS‑derived ionic conductivity in Li‑chloride solid electrolyte samples.

In DC polarization measurements with ion‑blocking electrodes, a measured transference number ti close to 1 indicates predominantly ionic conduction, whereas ti much less than 1 indicates significant electronic leakage.

In this dataset, high levels of Y3+ doping can lead to formation of Li3YCl6 impurity phases (Y3+ “diverting” into Li3YCl6).
The sample Li1.5Mn0.7Y0.2Ta0.1Cl4 measured an ionic conductivity of 2.08e-05 S/cm in this dataset despite containing approximately 25% Li3YCl6 impurity.
Within this dataset, compositions with moderate Y3+ combined with a concurrent high-valent dopant preserved the spinel phase and yielded high ionic conductivity.

In this dataset, Ta5+-only compositions at nominal Li ≈ 1.4–1.5 exhibited good ionic conductivity, and their conductivity was sensitive to cation ordering; low-angle diffraction features were reduced near 350–400 °C.
The dataset indicates an empirically favored Li-vacancy range near Li ≈ 1.4–1.5 that is associated with higher ionic conductivity.
Large, polarizable Y3+ ions introduce local lattice softening and a size mismatch on the octahedral 16d sites of the spinel structure (mechanistic explanation).

Ta5+ substitution increases charge contrast and random fields that disrupt Li/metal cation ordering, which enlarges effective Li‑migration bottlenecks in the soft chloride framework (mechanistic explanation).

In this experimental campaign, compositions with Li ≈ 1.5 and V3+ ≈ 0.15–0.2 plus a small high‑valent dopant (Nb5+ or Ta5+) in Mn-containing spinel hosts were observed to optimize ionic conductivity and to minimize formation of the Li6VCl8 impurity phase.

In this dataset, stronger cation mixing on the octahedral sublattice correlated with fewer low-angle superlattice features and higher ionic conductivity; Sc-containing and V/Ta-tuned samples were given as examples exhibiting this correlation.
Within spinel crystal chemistry, Mn2+ and Ni2+ exhibit an octahedral site preference (occupying octahedral coordination sites such as the 16d position in Fd-3m spinel lattices).
The Fd-3m spinel lattice contains edge- and face-sharing polyhedra that are structural features relevant to Li+ migration pathways in spinel solid electrolytes.
In this campaign, the V/Ta aliovalent doping motif at approximately Li ≈ 1.5 was identified as a best-performing aliovalent motif for improving conductivity in Mn-based spinel chloride samples.

From patterns learned in this experimental campaign, introducing V3+ at approximately 0.15–0.20 (i.e., ~15–20 mol fraction) into Li2MCl4-type spinels improves ionic conductivity (σ) but carries a risk of forming the Li6VCl8 secondary phase unless a small amount of Nb5+ (or Ta5+) is co-introduced.

Optimizing the V:Nb ratio in prior experiments restored single-phase spinel and increased ionic conductivity; for example, the composition Li1.7Mn0.85Nb0.03V0.15Cl4 exhibited higher conductivity than the analogous composition with Nb = 0.05.
Within this dataset, Li stoichiometry near Li ≈ 1.5 consistently correlates with higher ionic conductivity compared to Li2 compositions in the chloride spinel samples studied.
Co2+ has a strong octahedral site preference in oxide/chloride coordination environments (i.e., Co2+ strongly prefers octahedral coordination sites).

In the studied Li chloride spinel systems, the combination of a strongly octahedral-preferring 2+ cation (Co2+) with aliovalent V3+/Nb5+ yields high charge/size disorder on the 16d (octahedral) sublattice, which suppresses Li/M ordering (manifesting as low-angle superlattice reflections) that is associated with reduced ionic mobility.

Li vacancies in these chloride spinel frameworks percolate through the three-dimensional tetrahedral–octahedral network of the soft Cl sublattice, a percolating vacancy network that lowers Li-ion migration barriers.

In this dataset/campaign, purposeful deviation from M = 1.0 (forming stuffed/deficient inverse spinel variants) is observed in space group Fd-3m as the composition Li12.8Mn9.6Cl32 (i.e., Li1.6Mn1.2Cl4), and such deviations can alter defect chemistry in these spinel chloride materials.

In prior experiments from this dataset, incorporating V3+ at approximately 0.2 per formula unit is associated with enhanced ionic conductivity (σ), provided the competing Li6VCl8 phase is suppressed by maintaining overall charge balance and Li deficiency.

In Li2MCl4-type spinel chloride compositions with extra Ni2+ occupancy on the 16d (octahedral) network, the additional Ni2+ occupancy modifies Li octahedral-site occupancy/availability and steers Li into a more highly disordered tetrahedral–octahedral manifold.

V3+ substitution in these spinel chloride lattices generates random fields that, together with cation-site disorder (e.g., from Ni2+ on 16d), can reduce correlated Li ordering and open alternative Li-percolation pathways in the soft chloride lattice.

Lithium deficiency in spinel-type frameworks (for example Li = 1.5 per formula unit versus Li = 2) typically introduces lithium vacancies that facilitate Li+ transport via vacancy-mediated mechanisms.

In crystallography, the presence of unindexed reflections relative to a high-symmetry model (such as Fd-3m for spinel) is commonly interpreted as evidence for cation or vacancy ordering or subtle symmetry lowering (i.e., formation of a superstructure) rather than a perfectly disordered high-symmetry phase.

High Li+ conductivity in inverse spinels depends on partial Li/transition-metal disorder and an appropriate distribution of Li vacancies across the three-dimensional network of Li polyhedra; ordering of cations and/or Li vacancies can disrupt Li hopping connectivity, increase migration barriers, and lower ionic conductivity.

The composition Li1.5M1Cl4 contains fewer lithium atoms per formula unit than Li2M1Cl4, which implies charge compensation via a higher average transition-metal valence and therefore a greater population of lithium vacancies in the structure.

At lower synthesis temperatures (for example 400 °C), lithium vacancies and the transition-metal sublattice are more likely to order; such ordering can produce superlattice reflections in XRD and can suppress ionic conductivity relative to a disordered state.
Increasing synthesis temperature is a standard experimental method to increase configurational disorder in solid solutions.
All entries in this dataset target the Li2−yM1±xCl4 inverse‑spinel halide framework (anion ccp, Fd-3m reference).

In the dataset, samples were synthesized by the same solid‑state route and room‑temperature ionic conductivity (σRT) was measured on pressed pellets in N2, enabling fair cross‑comparison across samples.

In this Co‑based inverse‑spinel subset of the dataset, room‑temperature conductivities for spinel‑indexed compositions generally fall in approximately 10^-7–10^-6 S/cm, and rise toward a few 10^-6 S/cm when disorder and/or Li vacancies are present.

In spinel structures with a close-packed Cl sublattice, Li+ migrates through a three-dimensional network of tetrahedral and octahedral sites via 8a–16c–8a and 16d–48f–16d hops (established spinel transport mechanism).

Vacancies and cation disorder generally lower Li+ migration barriers and improve percolation up to an optimum, whereas excessive vacancies can induce long-range ordering or phase separation that typically degrades ionic transport (general materials-physics principle).

Inverse spinel chlorides commonly exhibit stronger cation/vacancy ordering at lower synthesis temperatures due to reduced configurational entropy and slower cation exchange.
Cation/vacancy ordering in inverse spinel chlorides can reduce the connectivity of Li migration pathways and increase Li+ migration barriers, thereby lowering ionic conductivity.
Introducing a small amount of a heterovalent cation such as Sc3+ is a known strategy to frustrate cation/vacancy ordering and promote configurational disorder in these types of materials.

Higher synthesis temperatures typically increase configurational disorder in spinel-like lithium halides, and increased configurational disorder can enhance ionic conductivity.

Multi-cation disorder and local structural distortions can flatten Li site energy landscapes and enhance three-dimensional connectivity of Li-ion migration pathways in spinel-type Li2MCl4 structures.

In halide ionic conductors (from prior literature/established principles), increasing lattice polarizability and introducing cation/vacancy disorder can lower Li+ migration barriers and thereby improve Li+ mobility.

In this dataset, Sn2+ solubility and site preference in the chloride inverse spinel structure are not established (i.e., the dataset does not determine whether Sn2+ is soluble or which cation site it prefers).
In samples with xBi = 0.10 synthesized at 400 °C with a 12 h hold, Bi3+ exceeds its solid solubility and/or partially volatilizes as a chloride, driving formation of a LiCl secondary phase.

LiCl is a poor lithium-ion conductor at room temperature, and even modest amounts of LiCl distributed at grain boundaries can depress bulk or percolative Li+ transport in polycrystalline materials.

Many metal chlorides exhibit appreciable volatility in the ~300–500 °C temperature window; reducing synthesis temperature generally lowers vapor pressures of volatile chlorides and can mitigate their loss.

The dataset observation that LiCl appears at xBi = 0.10 but not at xBi = 0.05 for samples processed at 400 °C suggests that at xBi = 0.10 Bi either exceeds the solid solubility limit in the spinel at 400 °C and/or undergoes partial Bi–chloride loss during the 12 h hold, and those processes can drive LiCl exsolution.

LiCl exsolution or Bi–chloride loss that reduces the effective spinel phase fraction can lower the connectivity of the spinel network (and can alter Li-vacancy distribution), which is consistent with the observed large drop in room-temperature ionic conductivity for the xBi = 0.10 sample.
The commonly cited formation window for Li–halide spinels is approximately 300–500 °C.

Li2MgCl4 synthesized at 450 °C is mostly spinel (Fd-3m) with a spinel phase fraction of 0.9616 and room-temperature ionic conductivity σRT = 3.16e-06 S/cm (reported as the high-σ baseline for a divalent M2+ spinel synthesized at high temperature).

Li2Zn0.5Mg0.5Cl4 synthesized at 250 °C is mostly spinel with a spinel fraction of 0.8648 but contains ZnCl2 with fraction 0.1352, has a higher Rwp = 12.85% with multiple missing XRD peaks, and a very low room-temperature ionic conductivity σRT = 1.0e-08 S/cm.

Li2Zn0.5Mg0.5Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C shows an increased room-temperature ionic conductivity of 1.88e-07 S/cm (approximately 19× higher than the 250 °C sample), improved Rwp = 7.43% with fewer missing XRD peaks, but a reduced spinel fraction of 0.5995 with the appearance of Li2ZnCl4 (Pnma) and ZnCl2 comprising roughly 0.40 of the sample.

For the Zn-containing Li2Zn0.5Mg0.5Cl4 system studied here, higher synthesis temperature (400 °C vs 250 °C) is associated with formation of non-spinel phases (Li2ZnCl4 and ZnCl2), which reduces the measured spinel fraction.

The 250 °C Li2Zn0.5Mg0.5Cl4 sample contains ZnCl2 consistent with incomplete reaction, which coincides with its suppressed Li+ mobility (very low σRT) despite having a higher measured spinel fraction than the 400 °C sample.

Raising synthesis temperature generally promotes cation disorder in spinel structures, and increased cation disorder tends to lower Li+ migration barriers by improving connectivity of octahedral–tetrahedral–octahedral (oct–tet–oct) Li-ion pathways.

Within the observations and interpretation reported here, there are two competing temperature-dependent effects for Zn-containing Li2MCl4 spinels: (A) beneficial increase in cation disorder with temperature that can enhance Li+ mobility, and (B) detrimental decomposition at higher temperature to non-spinel phases that reduces the spinel fraction and can lower conductivity.

In the reported experiments, the 400 °C Li2Zn0.5Mg0.5Cl4 sample exhibited lower XRD Rwp (7.43%) and fewer missing peaks compared to the 250 °C sample (Rwp = 12.85%), indicating improved XRD agreement at higher synthesis temperature for this composition.
A synthesis temperature of 350 °C lies within the 300–700 °C temperature range that is described here as a typical window for halide solid-state reactions.

Rietveld analysis of the sample synthesized at 250 °C indicates phases spinel (Fd-3m) (0.8648 fraction) and ZnCl2 (0.1352 fraction) with Rwp = 12.85% and multiple missing XRD peaks (examples: 31.82°, 34.91°, 36.50°, 49.86°, 31.48°, 15.09°).

The 250 °C product shows a notable ZnCl2 impurity and poorer XRD agreement (higher Rwp and more missing peaks) compared to the compositionally similar, spinel-rich 400 °C sample.

In this Zn-containing system, heating Li2Zn0.5Mg0.5Cl4 to 400 °C partially increases cation disorder, which raises ionic conductivity (σ).

The Zn-containing Li2Zn0.5Mg0.5Cl4 samples (250–400 °C) exhibit substantially lower room-temperature ionic conductivity (~10^-8–10^-7 S/cm) than the Zn-free spinel-rich references synthesized at 450 °C (σRT on the order of 10^-6 S/cm).
Heating the Zn-containing composition to 400 °C is associated with segregation/decomposition into Li2ZnCl4 and ZnCl2 phases, as evidenced by the presence of these phases in the 400 °C sample.

The observed increase in conductivity from 250 °C to 400 °C for Li2Zn0.5Mg0.5Cl4 occurs despite a lower measured spinel fraction at 400 °C, indicating that the conductivity gain is not simply due to higher spinel content and instead implicating temperature-driven changes within the spinel (for example, increased cation disorder and/or increased defect concentration) as dominant contributors to conductivity.

In spinel-type lithium conductors, Li+ transport benefits from a connected network of partially occupied Li sites and a finite concentration of Li vacancies; conversely, overly ordered cation distributions and scarce Li vacancies increase migration barriers and can impede Li+ migration pathways.

The dataset observations suggest that the Zn-containing lattice in Li2Zn0.5Mg0.5Cl4 is more prone to cation ordering and/or has an insufficient population of mobile Li defects when synthesized at low temperature, which suppresses Li+ percolation relative to Zn-free spinel analogues.

In this dataset, Zr4+ incorporated alone into Li–Mg spinel compositions can depress ionic conductivity and induce impurity phases, whereas co-doping with stabilizers such as Fe2+ can recover a clean spinel phase and raise conductivity (example comparison at 400 °C: Li1.6Fe0.2Mg0.6Zr0.2 vs Li1.6Mg0.8Zr0.2).
In this dataset, In3+ substituted into the spinel host on its own forms a spinel-majority phase without severe phase separation (example: Li1.8Mg0.8In0.2).

Aliovalent substitution in Li–halide spinels (e.g., introducing higher-valent cations such as Zr4+ or In3+ into a divalent host) creates Li vacancies through charge compensation; consequently tuning the average transition-metal charge to 2.6 and setting Li = 1.4 is charge-balanced and introduces mobile Li vacancies.

Within this dataset, the compositional pattern described as 'spinel + modest Y3+ boundary' performed best among examined patterns (i.e., delivered the highest observed room-temperature ionic conductivities).
Ni, Zn, heavy Sn, and Cr are recognized as problematic dopants to avoid for these chloride spinel systems (as stated in the proposal rationale).
In this dataset, Zr incorporated without Fe has been observed sometimes to lower ionic conductivity (noted as an uncertainty in prior dataset observations).

In this dataset, increasing Y content via a larger Li3YCl6 fraction from z = 0.2 to z = 0.33 increased measured ionic conductivity from approximately 1e-5 S/cm to approximately 2e-5 S/cm while the spinel phase remained the majority at z ≈ 0.33.
In this dataset, the composition Li1.67Mg0.67Y0.33 exhibited an ionic conductivity of 2.33e-05 S/cm and a measured spinel fraction of 0.655.

In this dataset, Fe2+ co-doping in Zr-containing systems produced a single-phase spinel and higher ionic conductivity for Li1.6Fe0.2Mg0.6Zr0.2 compared to the Zr-only composition when synthesized at 400 °C.

Observations in this dataset indicate that Fe co-doping has previously stabilized the spinel phase in these chloride spinel systems.

In this dataset, Zr4+–Fe2+ co-doping stabilized a spinel-only phase and produced higher ionic conductivity compared to Zr-only doped samples; an example composition showing this behavior is Li1.6Fe0.2Mg0.6Zr0.2 synthesized at 400 °C.

In this dataset, Ta5+ or Nb5+ improved ionic conductivity when paired with an effective divalent host and disordering co-dopants (for example Fe2+), whereas their performance in samples lacking Fe was mixed.
Within this dataset, Hf4+ has not been as extensively validated as Zr4+ (i.e., fewer validated data points for Hf4+ relative to Zr4+).

Cu2+ in octahedral coordination commonly exhibits Jahn–Teller distortions (a crystallographic fact about Cu2+ behavior in octahedral sites).

Jahn–Teller distortions associated with octahedral Cu2+ can break subtle cation/vacancy ordering and increase configurational disorder, effects that can in principle facilitate Li+ transport in a disordered spinel framework (general mechanistic assertion from crystallography/solid-state chemistry).

In this dataset, ordering introduced by certain higher-valent or specific co-dopants (examples noted include Nb5+ or Ni2+ at lower synthesis temperatures) has been observed to lower ionic conductivity.

Compositions with Li approximately 1.7 (corresponding to y ≈ 0.3 Li vacancies) frequently give the highest ionic conductivity values in this experimental dataset.

The specific V3+ + Hf4+ co-doping combination at y ≈ 0.3 has not been tested in this dataset (i.e., this exact compositional pairing is absent from the experimental records).

V-containing chemistries in this dataset can form non-spinel V–Cl impurity phases if reaction progress or structural disorder is incomplete, an observation associated with lower-temperature syntheses.

Across multiple compositions in this dataset, mixed aliovalent (3+,4+) co-doping at y ≈ 0.3 correlates with improved ionic conductivity, consistent with increased Li/M site disorder within the inverse spinel framework reported in these experiments.

Within this dataset, compositions containing V3+ combined with Mn2+ produce conductive spinel phases, with conductivity improving as Li content is decreased toward approximately Li ≈ 1.2–1.4 (i.e., higher vacancy).
In this dataset, doping Co-host spinel compositions with Ta5+ preserved the spinel phase but did not increase ionic conductivity (σ).
The effect of Ta5+ substitution within a Mn–V–Fe spinel framework at high Li vacancy has not been tested in this dataset.
In this dataset, Ni, Zn, and Cr-containing compositions either reduce ionic conductivity or destabilize the spinel phase.
Compositions with Y content at or above 0.2 in this campaign tend to form Li3YCl6 instead of the targeted spinel phase.
Analysis of multiple entries in this dataset shows that cation/vacancy ordering correlates with extra low-angle misfit features in diffraction and with depressed ionic conductivity (σ).
Ta can segregate in these chemistries; Ta-containing chloride impurity phases (TaClx) were observed in at least one Ni-based co-doped sample in this dataset.
Compositions with V ≈ 0.5 are near composition ranges where the separate phase Li6VCl8 can appear in other (non-dataset) chemistries.
In this dataset, the spinel composition Li1.2Mn0.5V0.6Cl4 (space group Fd-3m) exhibits an ionic conductivity of 1.52e-05 S/cm.
In this dataset, the spinel composition Li1.4Mn0.4V0.6Cl4 exhibits an ionic conductivity of 4.18e-06 S/cm.
Within this experimental campaign, Mn–V spinels with high V3+ content (and correspondingly higher Li-vacancy content) give the best spinel conductivities observed in the dataset.
In this dataset, the Fe–V composition Li1.5Fe0.5V0.5Cl4 has an ionic conductivity of 2.21e-06 S/cm and displays a minor secondary (non-spinel) phase.
Across samples in this dataset, Co- and Ni-centric host compositions are generally less conductive compared to the better-performing hosts.
Across this dataset, inclusion of Zn or Cr consistently degrades either spinel phase stability or the ionic conductivity (σ) of the materials.

More Li vacancies (approximately y ≈ 0.6) enhance connectivity of the 8a–16c–8a Li migration network in halide spinels, and mixed 2+/3+ charges on the 16d sites frustrate cation ordering; both effects are known to reduce Li-ion migration barriers in halide spinels.
Fe-containing systems can exhibit subtle phase competition; in this dataset that is exemplified by the minor non-spinel phase observed in Li1.5Fe0.5V0.5Cl4.

High-V (high V-content) synthesis regimes can risk segregation into Li6VCl8-type phases in some host chemistries (i.e., the high-V regime has been associated with Li6VCl8-type segregation in some hosts).

In this dataset, the composition Li1.9Co0.9Y0.1Cl4 was observed as a single-phase spinel and exhibited an ionic conductivity of 1.87e-06 S/cm.

In this dataset, low-level Y3+ substitution at ~10% can remain within the spinel field, whereas higher Y concentrations drive formation of Li3YCl6 and shift ion transport outside the spinel framework.
In this dataset, substitution of Sc3+ into Co- and Fe-containing spinel hosts produced conductivities on the order of ~10^-5 S/cm, supporting a vacancy/disorder mechanism that increased σ.
Across the dataset, Mn-containing spinels were observed to be generally more promising (higher performing) than Zn- or Cr-containing spinels.
In the dataset, Ni-containing compositions tended to show Ni segregation as NiCl2 rather than forming the intended spinel.
In this dataset, the highest-σ Mn–V examples had vacancy levels y approximately in the range 0.4–0.8, so a vacancy level of y=0.2 is lower than those highest-σ examples.

In spinel lithium-halide systems, introducing modest amounts of high-valent dopants (e.g., Ta5+) increases average transition-metal charge and can create controlled Li vacancies/disorder in the Li sublattice.
A slight metal deficiency together with modest Li non-stoichiometry can enhance Li-sublattice connectivity/percolation in spinel-derived lithium halide electrolytes.

In this dataset, high vacancy content (lower Li) correlates with higher ionic conductivity in Mn-based spinel chloride compositions when the spinel framework is retained; for example, the composition Li1.2Mn0.5V0.6 showed an ionic conductivity of 1.52e-05 S/cm.
In this dataset, Co-only compositions exhibited ordering/orthorhombic signatures and low ionic conductivity unless heterovalent dopants were introduced to disrupt that ordering.
In this dataset, small amounts of Co mixed into Mn/Fe host compositions were tolerated within the spinel structure (i.e., small Co content was spinel-tolerant).

In this dataset, Zr4+ substitution in Co-only hosts produced spinel phases but with modest ionic conductivity; for example, Li1.6Co0.8Zr0.2 exhibited an ionic conductivity of approximately 2e-07 S/cm.
In this dataset, Zr4+ helped form spinel in Co-only systems but did not, by itself, elevate ionic conductivity.

In the current dataset, In3+ co-doping can produce high intrinsic spinel conductivity without relying on Li3YCl6-phase boundaries: specifically, Li1.5Mg0.6In0.3Zr0.1Cl4 was observed as a single spinel phase and exhibited an ionic conductivity of 1.03e-05 S/cm, which is higher than the Mg-only baseline Li2MgCl4 (≈3.16e-06 S/cm) measured in this campaign.

In this dataset, Sc3+ tends to form Li3ScCl6-type phases rather than spinel at similar synthesis temperatures: examples include Li1.85Zn0.425Mg0.425Sc0.15Cl4 and Li1.5Mg0.7Zr0.2Sc0.1Cl4, which crystallized as Li3ScCl6-type phases.

In the current experimental campaign, Fe2+ co-doping was observed to stabilize the spinel phase and often improve ionic conductivity relative to Mg-only systems; for example, Li1.4Fe0.2Mg0.6Ta0.2Cl4 showed an ionic conductivity of 6.1e-06 S/cm.
In this dataset Li1.35Mg0.7Mn0.3Zr0.1Nb0.05Cl4 was identified as a single spinel-phase sample and exhibited an ionic conductivity of 3.16e-06 S/cm.
Multi-cation disorder was observed to introduce low-angle misfits in measured samples from this dataset, as was seen for the In+Zr-containing spinel sample.

Based on the current dataset, an In3+-enabled single-spinel route (i.e., In3+ co-doping yielding single-phase spinel without Y) is supported by the measured results as the most promising intrinsic (non-Y) path for achieving higher ionic conductivity.
From outside this dataset, In3+ is known to sometimes stabilize Li3InCl6 in other chloride systems (a phenomenon not observed for the cited dataset sample but reported in other chloride chemistries).

Within this experimental dataset, Y3+ consistently correlates with higher ionic conductivity (σ) when Li3YCl6 appears as a minority phase: Li1.8Mg0.8Y0.2Cl4 has σ = 1.06e-05 S/cm with ~7–13 wt% Li3YCl6 after synthesis at 450–500 °C; Li1.7Mg0.7Y0.3Cl4 shows σ = 1.29e-05–1.77e-05 S/cm; Li1.67Mg0.67Y0.33Cl4 shows σ = 2.33e-05 S/cm; Li1.6Mg0.6Y0.4Cl4 shows σ = 2.52e-05 S/cm but the spinel fraction is <50% in that sample.
In this dataset, compositions without Y do not reproduce the ~1e-5–2e-5 S/cm conductivity regime even when vacancy content is matched; for example, Li1.6Mg1.2Cl4 exhibits σ = 4.55e-06 S/cm.
Across the dataset, Fe-containing spinel hosts are observed to be robust and can deliver moderate ionic conductivity (σ) in the studied Li–M–Cl spinel compositions.
Within the dataset, Cu-containing spinel-only compositions show depressed ionic conductivity; for example, Li1.6Mg0.6Cu0.2Nb0.2Cl4 exhibits σ = 9.41e-08 S/cm.
The selection rationale states the allowed/assumed cation valences for charge-balance considerations as Fe2+, Cu+, Y3+, Mn2+, and Mg2+.
In this dataset, compositions with Y ≈ 0.2 that form mixtures of spinel and Li3YCl6 reproducibly show ionic conductivities around 1×10⁻⁵ S/cm.

In this dataset, small amounts of Nb5+ coexisting with Y were observed to produce a spinel-majority product at higher synthesis temperatures and were associated with elevated ionic conductivity.
Cu2+ is Jahn–Teller active (chemical property of the Cu2+ ion).
In prior Mg–Nb spinel samples within this dataset, the presence of Cu2+ was observed to reduce ionic conductivity.
Li1.4Mn0.8Nb0.2Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C is a single-phase spinel with ionic conductivity of 2.63e-05 S/cm (observed in this dataset).
Within this dataset, compositions with Nb5+ near 0.2 and Li ≈ 1.4 yield robust ionic conductivity and clean spinel phases.
Within this dataset, substitution by 4+ cations alone (Zr4+, Hf4+) typically yields modest ionic conductivity on the order of ~1e-5 S/cm.
Within this dataset, when 4+ substitution is coupled with an appropriate vacancy level and broader 16d-site cation mixing, ionic conductivity can improve relative to 4+ substitution alone.

Within this dataset, multi-cation mixing on the 16d site (for example Fe2+/Mn2+/Ni2+ plus a small 4+ fraction) tends to frustrate cation ordering, and this frustrated ordering correlates with lower ionic conductivity.
In this dataset, Zr4+-bearing spinels sometimes show extra or missing diffraction peaks indicative of subtle deviations from the expected phase.
Li2Cr0.5Mn0.5Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C exhibits an unusually high room-temperature ionic conductivity (σRT) relative to typical Cr-containing spinels.
Samples of Li2Cr0.5Mn0.5Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C show coexistence of spinel with substantial amounts of LiCl and Li2CrCl4.
The coexistence of spinel with substantial LiCl and Li2CrCl4 in these samples produces Li-deficient (vacancy-rich) spinel regions and heterointerfaces.

These Li-deficient spinel regions and heterointerfaces increase mobile Li defect concentrations and reduce Li-ion migration barriers, yielding a macroscopic ionic conductivity much higher than that of single-phase Cr-bearing spinels.
Cr-containing spinel chloride materials characteristically exhibit room-temperature ionic conductivities on the order of 10^-8 to 10^-7 S/cm.

Li2Cr0.5Mn0.5Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C is multiphase by XRD with phase fractions spinel (Fd-3m) = 0.5674, LiCl (Fm-3m) = 0.2432, and Li2CrCl4 (C12/m1) = 0.1894, and this sample shows room-temperature ionic conductivity σRT = 6.92e-06 S/cm.

The spinel fit for the Li2Cr0.5Mn0.5Cl4 (400 °C) sample exhibits extra low-angle XRD intensity (for example at 14.58° 2θ), indicating deviation from the ideal Fd-3m spinel model consistent with ordering or structural modulation in the spinel phase.
Li1.5Mn0.5Cr0.5Cl4 (spinel fraction 0.7068) measured in this dataset has room-temperature ionic conductivity σRT = 6.76e-08 S/cm.
Li1.5Fe0.5Cr0.5Cl4 (noted as spinel-only in this dataset) has room-temperature ionic conductivity in the range σRT = 3.37e-08–4.22e-07 S/cm in this campaign's measurements.
Li1.5Cr0.5Mg0.5Cl4 (spinel-only in this dataset) has room-temperature ionic conductivity σRT = 1.48e-07 S/cm according to these measurements.
The Li2CrCl4 baseline mixture measured in this dataset shows room-temperature ionic conductivity σRT = 2.72e-07 S/cm.
Single-phase or spinel-dominant Cr-containing systems observed in this dataset typically display room-temperature ionic conductivities on the order of 10^-8–10^-7 S/cm.
LiCl at room temperature is a poor Li+ conductor (LiCl is known to have low ionic conductivity at ambient conditions).
In spinel structures, increased lithium-vacancy concentration and cation/Li sublattice disorder generally lower Li+ migration barriers (a general solid-state ionics principle).

Coexistence of a separate LiCl phase can sequester lithium into that phase and thereby render the remaining spinel Li-deficient (Li2−y), which would increase lithium vacancy concentration in the spinel matrix (mechanistic statement about defect chemistry at phase coexistence).

Heterointerfaces such as spinel/LiCl boundaries can alter defect concentrations via space-charge effects and can potentially boost Li+ mobility across those interfaces (established interfacial defect/space-charge behavior in solid-state ionics).

Within this dataset, heating samples to 450 °C often drives reactions closer to completion and increases spinel fraction; as an example from these experiments, Li1.5Fe0.5Cr0.5Cl4 becomes spinel-only when heated to 450 °C.

The temperature 450 °C lies within an established 300–700 °C window commonly used for halide solid-state synthesis and is viewed as a condition that mitigates undue volatilization risk (general synthesis knowledge).

The observed room-temperature conductivity of the multiphase Li2Cr0.5Mn0.5Cl4 (6.92e-06 S/cm) is higher than would be expected from a simple volume-weighted sum of the measured conductivities of its identified constituent crystalline phases (spinel, LiCl, Li2CrCl4) given their reported phase fractions in this dataset.
In the inverse spinel Li2−yM1±xCl4 framework (space group Fd-3m), Li transport is governed by the connected Li polyhedra and defect chemistry.
This dataset assesses synthesis outcomes using composition, synthesis_temperature, XRD phase fractions/misfit, and ionic conductivity (σ) measured at 25 °C.
The composition Li1.5Mn0.5Cr0.5Cl4 in this dataset is multiphase with an Fd-3m spinel phase fraction of 0.7068 and exhibits room-temperature ionic conductivity σRT = 6.76e-08 S/cm.
The composition Li1.5Fe0.5Cr0.5Cl4 (reported as spinel-only) in this dataset exhibits room-temperature ionic conductivity σRT = 3.37e-08 S/cm.
The composition Li1.5Cr0.5Mg0.5Cl4 (reported as spinel-only) in this dataset exhibits room-temperature ionic conductivity σRT = 1.0e-08 S/cm.
A Li2CrCl4-containing baseline sample (composition described as Li2CrCl4 + LiCl + CrCl2) in this dataset exhibits room-temperature ionic conductivity σRT = 2.72e-07 S/cm.

The sample Li2Cr0.5Mn0.5Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C in this dataset refines with a majority Fd-3m spinel fraction of 0.5674 (coexisting with LiCl and Li2CrCl4) and exhibits room-temperature ionic conductivity σRT = 6.92e-06 S/cm.

The measured σRT = 6.92e-06 S/cm for Li2Cr0.5Mn0.5Cl4 (400 °C) is roughly 1–2 orders of magnitude higher than the σRT values reported for the other Cr-containing spinel cases listed above in this dataset.

Within this dataset's contrast set of multiple Cr-containing compositions, the Li2Cr0.5Mn0.5Cl4 (400 °C) sample's conductivity lies far above the typical room-temperature σ range observed for Cr-bearing spinel systems under similar synthesis and measurement conditions.
The Li1.6Mg0.6Cu0.2Nb0.2Cl4 sample synthesized at 400 °C exhibited abnormally low ionic conductivity (σ).
X-ray diffraction (XRD) of the Li1.6Mg0.6Cu0.2Nb0.2Cl4 sample synthesized at 400 °C shows additional observed reflections that are not captured by the spinel (Fd-3m) model.

Low-temperature structural heterogeneity in Li1.6Mg0.6Cu0.2Nb0.2Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C—manifesting as either cation/vacancy ordering (symmetry lowering from the average Fd-3m) or minor secondary Cu–Cl–rich features—disrupts the 3D Li+ percolation network and/or blocks grain boundaries, thereby suppressing ionic conductivity.
Li1.6Mg0.6Cu0.2Nb0.2Cl4 synthesized at 400 °C has a room-temperature ionic conductivity σRT = 9.41e-08 S/cm, which is far below the spinel-only peers (~3–6e-06 S/cm) observed in this dataset.

Powder XRD of Li1.6Mg0.6Cu0.2Nb0.2Cl4 (synthesized at 400 °C) refines to a spinel model (space group Fd-3m, 1.0 wt fraction) but shows several observed peaks not indexed by the spinel model at 24.18°, 30.08°, 34.87°, 50.12°, 59.55°, and 84.08°, with a reported Rwp of 10.22%.
Spinel samples synthesized at 450 °C in this dataset (examples given: Li2MgCl4, Li1.6Mg1.2Cl4, Li1.5Mg0.7Zr0.2Sc0.1Cl4) exhibit room-temperature ionic conductivities in the ~3–5e-06 S/cm range.

Both Cu-containing samples in this study were synthesized at 400 °C and are outliers in conductivity within the dataset, having low σRT values of 4.0e-07 and 9.41e-08 S/cm, and both display nontrivial unindexed XRD features.

In powder XRD, extra observed reflections beyond an average Fd-3m spinel model typically indicate either minor unidentified phases or a symmetry-lowering superstructure (e.g., cation/vacancy ordering).
Minor unidentified phases or symmetry-lowering cation/vacancy ordering can disrupt Li+ migration pathways or introduce blocking grain-boundary features in spinel chloride solid electrolytes.
In inverse-spinel chloride materials, Li+ transport is aided by cation disorder and a well-connected Li-vacancy network within the close-packed Cl– sublattice.

Insufficient reaction or disorder at lower synthesis temperatures can preserve cation/vacancy ordering that raises Li-ion migration barriers and/or leave nanoscale secondary halide features at grain boundaries that impede ionic percolation; both types of structural heterogeneity can manifest as additional reflections not captured by an average Fd-3m spinel model.
A nominally single-phase inverse-spinel sample refined by XRD as spinel (space group Fd-3m) with a refined phase fraction of 1.0 at a synthesis temperature of 400 °C.

The XRD pattern for this sample is missing several expected peaks (examples at 30.08°, 34.87°, and 50.12°) and the refinement yielded a moderate Rwp of 10.22%, consistent with structural mismatch and/or subtle deviations from the ideal Fd-3m structure.

In inverse spinel chloride materials, aliovalent higher-valence substitution (e.g., Bi3+) creates lithium vacancies (the compositions discussed have y = 0.2 Li vacancies associated with Bi3+ substitution).
The Ca2+ ionic radius is larger than the Mg2+ ionic radius, so substituting Ca2+ for Mg2+ can strain the cation sublattice relative to Mg2+-only compositions.

Ca2+ substitution combined with Li-vacancy formation can promote cation/vacancy ordering or symmetry lowering from the ideal Fd-3m spinel; such ordering commonly produces additional or superstructure reflections in diffraction data and can suppress Li+ percolation pathways, lowering ionic conductivity.

Higher synthesis temperatures generally increase cation and Li-site disorder, reduce ordering signatures (e.g., weaken superstructure/missing peaks), and can raise ionic conductivity in ordered spinel chloride systems.

If Y3+ partitions out of the spinel to form Li3YCl6 at higher temperature, the remaining spinel will have reduced heterovalent substitution (fewer M3+ in the spinel), which reduces Li-vacancy concentration and/or cation disorder and therefore increases migration barriers and lowers room-temperature ionic conductivity.

In inverse-spinel chloride compounds, lithium ions and lithium vacancies occupy a three-dimensional network of tetrahedral and octahedral sites in the spinel framework.

At lower synthesis temperatures, spinel chlorides can develop long-range cation and Li-vacancy ordering that produces superlattice reflections at low XRD angles and reduces Li+ percolation through the structure.

In the reported dataset observations for Li1.4Mg0.8Ta0.2Cl4, increasing synthesis temperature correlated with the disappearance of low-angle XRD misfit features and with higher ionic conductivity, consistent with increased configurational disorder at higher temperature.

Isovalent substitution on the high-valent (5+) sublattice — for example mixing two isovalent 5+ cations such as Ta5+ and Nb5+ — perturbs site-preference, ionic-size, and electrostatic regularity on the octahedral network and is a commonly used strategy to frustrate or suppress long-range ordering in spinel-like frameworks.
In this dataset, Sc3+ co-doping at 400 °C coincided with formation of Li3ScCl6 as a secondary phase.
Because Sc3+ has a lower formal charge than Ta5+, substituting Sc3+ for a 5+ cation introduces a charge imbalance (charge mismatch) relative to the original 5+ sublattice occupancy.

Under those same conditions (400 °C, Nb5+ = 0.05), low-angle superstructure features appear in diffraction data for the Li2−y(Mn,V,Nb)Cl4 samples.

In spinel families, Zn2+ commonly prefers tetrahedral coordination (occupying tetrahedral sites preferentially).

Zn2+ preference for tetrahedral coordination can drive cation redistribution between tetrahedral and octahedral sites in spinel structures, increasing Li/M site disorder and altering the connectivity of Li diffusion pathways (the 8a–16d network).
Increased Li-site disorder and a better-connected three-dimensional Li diffusion pathway generally reduce migration barriers and increase ionic conductivity in solid electrolytes.
Secondary phases (e.g., NiCl2) can influence pellet microstructure (for example, grain-boundary contact and densification) and thereby affect the measured ionic conductivity.

Using charge neutrality with assumed oxidation states Mn2+ and Sc3+ (and Cl4-), the Li content in Li2–yCl4 compositions equals the positive-charge deficit required to balance the anions (i.e., Li stoichiometry is set by charge balance).

In spinel-type halides, higher Li-vacancy concentration generally facilitates Li+ hopping by providing more accessible empty sites within the connected tetrahedral–octahedral network (a standard principle of solid-state ionics cited as widely accepted behavior).

Cation ordering on octahedral sites in spinel frameworks can impede Li+ percolation by locally modifying Li-site energies and creating bottlenecks, a commonly reported effect in spinel-type materials.
