A spinel-dominant Y/Mn co-doped product Li1.8Fe0.6Mn0.2Y0.2Cl4 with Li3YCl6 fraction 0.084 exhibits σRT = 1.83e-05 S/cm.
Within this discovery dataset, the measured σRT = 9.48e-05 S/cm is an outlier compared with spinel-only analogues and has been flagged as an unusually high-conductivity case.
The unusually high σRT in this multiphase sample correlates with the presence of a substantial Li3YCl6 fraction (Li3YCl6 phase fraction 0.1834) in the mixture.
Li1.8Co0.4Fe0.4Sc0.2Cl4 inverse spinels synthesized at 500 °C exhibit an abnormally high room-temperature ionic conductivity (σRT).
In the Li2−y(Co,Fe,Sc)Cl4 samples synthesized at 500 °C, the Li1.8Co0.4Fe0.4Sc0.2Cl4 composition corresponds to y ≈ 0.2 set by Sc3+ substitution.
The y ≈ 0.2 composition in these Li2−y(Co,Fe,Sc)Cl4 inverse spinels provides a near-optimal Li-vacancy concentration that enables three-dimensional Li+ percolation.
Sc3+ substitution in these samples suppresses extra ordering observed in the undoped sample, as evidenced by unindexed XRD peaks at approximately 24.8° and 39.4° in the undoped material.
Suppression of the extra ordering by Sc3+ doping in Li1.8Co0.4Fe0.4Sc0.2Cl4 yields higher Li-site availability and lower effective Li-ion migration barriers.

Li1.8Co0.4Fe0.4Sc0.2Cl4 synthesized at 500 °C is a single-phase spinel and shows a room-temperature ionic conductivity σRT = 1.21e-05 S/cm, which is the highest value within the Co–Fe–Sc series reported in this dataset.

At a fixed synthesis temperature of 500 °C, measured room-temperature ionic conductivities for the Co–Fe–Sc series vary with Sc content as follows: 0% Sc → 1.42e-06 S/cm; 5% Sc → 3.17e-06 S/cm; 10% Sc → 4.8e-06 S/cm; 15% Sc → 1.17e-05 S/cm; 20% Sc → 1.21e-05 S/cm (values reported from this dataset).
Within the 500 °C Co–Fe–Sc dataset, conductivity rises strongly with Sc level, with a pronounced jump between 10% and 15% Sc and a plateau in conductivity between 15% and 20% Sc.
All Sc-doped samples in the 500 °C series refine to the spinel structure with space group Fd-3m according to X-ray diffraction refinements reported in this dataset.
The undoped (0% Sc) sample synthesized at 500 °C exhibits unindexed XRD peaks at approximately 24.78° and 39.42° 2θ, which are not present in the 10% Sc-doped sample in this dataset.

With increasing Sc content beyond 10% in the 500 °C series, the specific unindexed low-angle features seen in the undoped sample disappear (by 10% Sc) and different low-intensity misfit peaks appear at higher Sc levels, as observed by XRD in this dataset.

Based on the strong conductivity increase from 0% to 15% Sc and the conductivity plateau between 15% and 20% Sc at 500 °C, the dataset interpretation is that a composition with y ≈ 0.2 (Li1.8, i.e., 20% Sc) is near an optimum vacancy content for the Co–Fe host at 500 °C.

Aliovalent substitution of Sc3+ into Li2MCl4-type spinels introduces lithium vacancies by charge compensation (Sc3+ replacing a higher-valent cation reduces the required Li content to maintain charge neutrality), a general principle of aliovalent doping.

In close-packed halide spinel structures, Li+ migrates via adjacent tetrahedral–octahedral–tetrahedral site hops, and increasing the concentration of Li vacancies generally increases the number of accessible neighboring sites and can lower migration barriers up to an optimum vacancy concentration, beyond which additional vacancies or local distortions can reduce mobility (general ion-transport principle).
All samples in this dataset target the inverse-spinel chloride framework Li2−y M1±x Cl4 (space group Fd-3m) built on a cubic-close-packed Cl sublattice.
Li+/M site disorder and Li vacancies (generated by higher-valence substitution) generally reduce Li+ migration barriers in these spinel chloride materials.
Synthesis and measurement conditions are consistent across the dataset: solid-state synthesis with a 12 h hold in a Ni crucible, and room-temperature PEIS measurements at 600 MPa in N2.
The composition described belongs to the Co–Fe spinel family and contains heterovalent Sc3+ substitution that reduces the Li stoichiometry from Li2 to Li1.8, thereby introducing Li vacancies.
The dataset includes the parent composition Li2Co0.5Fe0.5Cl4 synthesized at both 450 °C and 500 °C, and Sc-doped variants at nominal 5%, 10%, and 15% Sc substitution for comparison.
The reported Sc-doped sample refines as a single-phase spinel (Fd-3m) with a refined phase fraction of 1.0 wt fraction and only modest misfit peaks in the diffraction pattern.
The same Sc-doped sample exhibits a room-temperature ionic conductivity σRT = 1.21e-05 S/cm as measured by PEIS under the stated conditions.
This σRT (1.21e-05 S/cm) is approximately 8.5× higher than the undoped Co–Fe parent synthesized at 500 °C, which has σRT = 1.42e-06 S/cm in this dataset.
The 1.21e-05 S/cm conductivity is higher than the 10% Sc analogue in this series (σRT = 4.8e-06 S/cm) and comparable to or slightly above the 15% Sc sample (σRT = 1.17e-05 S/cm).
The 1.21e-05 S/cm conductivity far exceeds typical conductivities observed in this dataset for other aliovalent substitutions (e.g., Zr4+, Ta5+, Nb5+), which lie in the ~1e-07–1e-06 S/cm range.

Given identical synthesis and measurement protocols and a clean spinel phase assignment, this sample's σRT is abnormally high relative to compositionally similar Co–Fe spinels and relative to the broader dataset.
Increasing Li-vacancy concentration within the spinel network can enhance Li+ transport (general trend consistent with the observations reported).

In this dataset, compositions with V3+ near 0.1–0.15 and Li ≈ 1.6–1.7 often produce a single‑phase spinel and exhibit ionic conductivity on the order of 1–3×10⁻⁵ S/cm; examples from the dataset include Li1.65Mn0.95V0.15Cl4 and Li1.6Mn0.9V0.2Cl4.

Within this dataset, excess V content or insufficient process control led to formation of the secondary phase Li6VCl8 and correspondingly lower ionic conductivity; for example, a sample reported as Li1.9Mn0.9V0.1Cl4 contained 8% Li6VCl8.

Data from this experimental campaign show that adding a modest amount (~0.1) of a pentavalent dopant (Nb5+) can tune lithium vacancy concentration without introducing ordering peaks when the Li content is not too low.

Cation mixing among Fe, Co, and Mn in samples from this dataset suppressed cation ordering and, after raising synthesis temperature appropriately (e.g., improvement observed for Fe-containing V spinel at 450 °C), restored or substantially improved ionic conductivity.

The dataset indicates that the risk of Li6VCl8 formation at 400 °C can be mitigated by lowering synthesis temperature (to ~350 °C) or by reducing high‑valent co‑dopant levels, although these changes can trade off against the degree of configurational disorder.

In this experimental dataset on lithium chloride spinel solid electrolytes, the composition Li1.5Mn0.5Y0.25In0.25Cl4 was observed as a single-phase spinel and reached an ionic conductivity of 1.19e-4 S/cm.
In this dataset, the composition Li1.5Mn0.3Fe0.2Y0.25In0.25Cl4 reached an ionic conductivity of 1.4e-4 S/cm but contained a Li6In2.12Cl12 side phase.

Patterns learned from this dataset indicate that the strongest ionic conductivity results come from compositions with Li ≈ 1.5 and mixed trivalent Y3+/In3+ content totaling approximately 0.5 (in Li2MCl4-type spinels).
Within this dataset, Y-only analogue compositions tend to deliver lower ionic conductivity or exhibit formation of Li3YCl6 side phases in Y-bearing mixes of lithium chloride spinel samples.
Within this dataset, In-only analogue compositions tend to deliver lower ionic conductivity or exhibit formation of Li6In2±xCl12 side phases in In-bearing lithium chloride spinel samples.
Mixing Y and In (co-doping) in Li ≈ 1.5 spinel compositions in this dataset appears to stabilize the spinel phase and sustain higher ionic conductivity compared to Y-only or In-only analogues.

In this dataset, vacancy-rich Mn–V spinels produced the highest ionic conductivities when a clean Fd-3m spinel phase was obtained; example samples include Li1.2Mn0.5V0.6Cl4 with conductivity 1.52e-05 S/cm and Li1.4Mn0.4V0.6Cl4 with conductivity 4.18e-06 S/cm.

In this dataset, adding Ni or Zn to compositions was detrimental to ionic conductivity: Ni-containing examples often contained NiCl2 and showed conductivities ≤1e-6 S/cm (example Li1.4Ni1.0V0.2Cl4 contained 0.52 wt% NiCl2 and had conductivity 2.1e-08 S/cm), and a Zn-rich sample Li2Co0.5Zn0.5Cl4 showed conductivity 1.32e-08 S/cm after synthesis at 500 °C with a strong ≈15° extra XRD peak.

Co and Fe host compositions in this dataset responded strongly to heterovalent vacancy creation by trivalent dopants: Sc3+-doped Co/Fe samples showed conductivities of 1.17e-05–1.21e-05 S/cm at Li ≈ 1.8–1.85.
In this dataset, single 4+/5+ dopants (Zr4+, Nb5+, Ta5+) in Co-host compositions tended to yield much lower conductivities, on the order of ~1e-7–1e-6 S/cm.

High vanadium content in Ni-host samples in this dataset can produce the Li6VCl8 secondary phase, whereas Co, Fe, and Mn hosts accommodated V without forming that Li6VCl8 impurity; for example, Li1.5Co0.7V0.2Nb0.1Cl4 was reported as a single spinel phase with conductivity 6.06e-07 S/cm.
In this dataset, a Li stoichiometry of approximately Li = 1.3 (y ≈ 0.7) corresponds to a vacancy-rich regime that correlated with the best-performing Mn–V conductor samples.

Low-level In3+ and Nb5+ substitution at 0.1 each in the proposed compositions are claimed (based on dataset trends) to introduce additional Li vacancies and to create 16d-site charge/size disorder in the spinel lattice.
The dataset showed that Sc-doping in Co/Fe hosts suggested a correlation where disorder and/or increased Li vacancies are associated with improved conductivities in those systems.
In this dataset, higher In content in Ni-based systems produced In-rich halide secondary phases (In-rich halides were observed at higher In levels in Ni-containing samples).
The proposed composition contains lower V (0.1) than the best Mn–V conductor examples in the dataset (which had V ≈ 0.5–0.6), as noted in the dataset comparisons.
The dataset indicates that multi-cation chemistries can lead to minor secondary phases (multi-cation compositions in the campaign sometimes produced minor secondary phases).
Within the dataset, Ni and Zn compositions were identified as the most problematic elements due to phase impurities and very low ionic conductivities.
Li2Co0.5Fe0.5Cl4 exhibited ionic conductivity of 1–3e-06 S/cm in the reported dataset.
Li1.85Co0.425Fe0.425Sc0.15Cl4 exhibited ionic conductivity of 1.17e-05 S/cm in the reported dataset.
Li1.8Co0.4Fe0.4Sc0.2Cl4 exhibited ionic conductivity of 1.21e-05 S/cm in the reported dataset.

In Co/Fe host compositions in this dataset, compositions near Li ≈ 2 showed modest ionic conductivity (~1–3×10⁻⁶ S/cm), while Sc3+ substitution that created Li vacancies increased conductivity to about 1×10⁻⁵ S/cm.
Li1.4Co0.8Nb0.2Cl4 exhibited ionic conductivity of 2.96e-07 S/cm in the reported dataset (single Nb5+ substitution in a Co host).
Co-doping Nb5+ with another aliovalent cation (example: V3+) in Co-host compositions in this dataset resulted in low conductivity (Li1.5Co0.7V0.2Nb0.1Cl4: ~6e-07 S/cm).
Ni and Zn additions in samples from this dataset correlated with formation of NiCl2 or strong low-angle extra diffraction peaks and with very low measured ionic conductivity.
Vanadium-containing compositions outside Co/Fe hosts in this dataset sometimes produced Li6VCl8 as an impurity phase.
Single Nb5+ substitution in Co-host compositions in this dataset did not achieve conductivities near 1×10⁻⁵ S/cm (NB: Li1.4Co0.8Nb0.2Cl4 measured at 2.96e-07 S/cm).
Co–Cr-like compositional behavior observed in the dataset was associated with suppression of ionic conductivity.
Moderate vacancy levels (target compositions approximating Li ≈ 1.7, vacancy y ≈ 0.3) correlated with improved conductivity in the Co/Fe–Sc systems reported in this dataset.
In this dataset, Co/Fe-based spinel samples showed strong benefits from vacancy/disorder; Sc3+-doped cases reached ionic conductivities of approximately 1e-5 S/cm.
In this dataset, the composition Li1.6Co0.8Zr0.2Cl4 (Zr4+ alone in a Co host) exhibited an ionic conductivity of about 2e-7 S/cm.
Ni-containing recipes in this dataset frequently segregated NiCl2 and showed ionic conductivities ≤ 1e-6 S/cm.
Zn-rich Co spinel samples in this dataset exhibited a strong ~15° diffraction peak and ionic conductivities ≤ 1e-7 S/cm.
Within this dataset, Mn additions in vacancy-rich spinels correlated with higher ionic conductivity; Mn–V systems reached up to 1.52e-5 S/cm at Li = 1.2.
High vacancy levels corresponding to Li ≈ 1.6 (y ≈ 0.4) correspond to the high-conductivity regimes observed in this dataset.
Prior Cu-containing Co systems in this dataset did not show clear conductivity gains.
In this dataset, long-range cation ordering correlated with poor ionic conductivity in several Co-based systems (examples given: Co/Cr and Co/Zn).
In this dataset, the highest ionic conductivities (σ) were observed in vacancy-rich spinel samples when strong cation disorder was present.
In this dataset, Co/Fe + Sc-doped compositions at Li ≈ 1.8 exhibited ionic conductivities of about 1.17e-05–1.21e-05 S/cm.
In this dataset, Mn–V compositions at Li = 1.2–1.5 reached ionic conductivities up to 1.52e-05 S/cm.
In this dataset, single 4+/5+ dopants in Co-host compositions (Zr4+, Ta5+, Nb5+) typically yielded ionic conductivities of only ~1e-7–1e-6 S/cm.

In this dataset, mixed aliovalent co-doping sometimes improved ionic conductivity relative to single-dopant baselines; for example, Li1.6Co0.8In0.1Ta0.1Cl4 showed σ = 1.29e-06 S/cm versus Li1.6Co0.8Zr0.2Cl4 which showed σ = 2.1e-07 S/cm.
In this dataset, addition of Zn and Ni was consistently harmful, producing either a strong low-angle superstructure or NiCl2 impurity phases.
In this dataset, co-doping with Hf4+ and Zr4+ has not yet achieved the Sc-level ionic conductivities observed for Sc-doped samples.
In this dataset, LiCl formation occurred in some mixed-dopant Co systems.

In this dataset, In3+ is the most reliable dopant for achieving single-phase inverse spinel with elevated ionic conductivity, as exemplified by Li1.5Mg0.5In0.5Cl4 (Fd-3m, 1.0 wt) with conductivity 1.55e-05 S/cm and Li1.5Mg0.6In0.3Zr0.1Cl4 (Fd-3m, 1.0 wt) with conductivity 1.03e-05 S/cm, both exceeding Mg-only baselines.
Ni- and Cu-containing spinels in this dataset frequently show very low ionic conductivity (for example, Li1.6Mg0.6Cu0.2Nb0.2Cl4: 9.41e-08 S/cm; Li1.4Mg0.2Ni0.2Y0.6Cl4: 2.96e-08 S/cm).
Zn-containing samples in this dataset promote formation of Li2ZnCl4 and exhibit poor ionic conductivity.

In this dataset, multi-cation and aliovalent co-doping tends to increase 16d-site disorder/vacancies and is correlated with higher ionic conductivity when problematic dopants are avoided, as illustrated by Li1.5Mg0.55Mn0.15Y0.2Nb0.1Cl4 (8.89e-06 S/cm) and several Ta-/Zr-/Sc-co-doped spinels reaching 3–7e-06 S/cm.
Confirmed high-ionic-conductivity In3+-doped cases in this dataset have vacancy parameter y approximately 0.5.
In-rich spinels observed in this dataset remain phase-pure at vacancy levels comparable to those discussed for the In3+-doped high-σ cases.

In spinel structures, increased 16d-site charge/configurational disorder and the formation of a three-dimensional Li-vacancy percolation network are widely accepted to lower Li+ migration barriers and thereby enhance Li+ ionic conductivity.

In this dataset, In3+ at approximately 0.3–0.5 stoichiometry stabilizes single-phase Li2MCl4-type spinel compositions and raises ionic conductivity to about 1e-5 S/cm; examples from the dataset are Li1.5Mg0.5In0.5Cl4 with σ = 1.55e-05 S/cm and Li1.5Mg0.6In0.3Zr0.1Cl4 with σ = 1.03e-05 S/cm.

In this dataset, compositions containing V3+ at 0.2 stoichiometry tend to produce a secondary Li6VCl8 phase and exhibit lowered ionic conductivity; for example, Li1.8Mg0.8V0.2Cl4 was refined as 80.99% spinel + 19.01% Li6VCl8 and showed σ = 1.05e-06 S/cm.
In this dataset, inclusion of Ni, Cu, Zn, or Cr in Li2MCl4 spinel compositions resulted in poor outcomes and formation of impurities.
In this dataset, compositions containing Zr4+ together with Mg2+ often produced LiCl and MgCl2 impurity phases or exhibited ordering signatures and correspondingly low ionic conductivity.

In this dataset, adding Fe2+ to Mg–Zr compositions stabilized clean single-phase spinel and improved ionic conductivity; specifically, Li1.6Fe0.2Mg0.6Zr0.2Cl4 was observed as a single-phase spinel with ionic conductivity 1.96e-06 S/cm, higher than Mg–Zr analogs.
In this dataset, incorporating V3+ at a fraction of 0.2 led to formation of the impurity phase Li6VCl8.
The dataset indicates that Fe incorporation helps stabilize Zr-containing spinels and elevates ionic conductivity relative to Mg–Zr baseline compositions.
In this dataset, a composition with vacancy parameter y = 0.1 (Li = 1.9) has a lower vacancy concentration than the highest-σ In-doped cases from the campaign.

In the dataset, the highest ionic conductivities cluster near Li ≈ 1.4–1.5 with substantial 3+ cation content and strong cation mixing on the 16d site; example compositions and measured conductivities include Li1.5Mn0.5Y0.25In0.25Cl4 (σ = 1.19e-04 S/cm), Li1.45Mn0.45Sc0.55 synthesized at 500 °C (σ = 1.44e-04 S/cm), and Li1.4Mn0.4Sc0.6 synthesized at 500 °C (σ = 1.28e-04 S/cm).
Within this dataset, a high Li-vacancy fraction combined with multi-cation mixing correlates with higher ionic conductivity (σ) in Li–M–Cl spinel compositions.
Y-containing compositions in this dataset often produce Li3YCl6 side phases that can dominate ionic transport; one example reported is Li1.5Mn0.7Y0.2Ta0.1Cl4 exhibiting such side-phase behavior.
A Mg-containing, V-spinel composition in the dataset, Li1.65Mn0.65Mg0.30V0.15Cl4, showed a conductivity increase from 2.52e-07 S/cm to 1.32e-05 S/cm when processed at 450 °C.
The dataset repeatedly shows that Zn-containing samples form Li2ZnCl4 secondary phases.
In-rich compositions in the dataset produced Li6In2−xCl12-type phases in several In-containing samples, with Li6In2−xCl12 appearing particularly in cases where the In fraction was about 0.25–0.4.

Observations in the dataset indicate that introducing 4+ or 5+ dopants into these chloride spinel compositions is associated with superlattice formation and secondary-phase risks (including low-angle features and segregation).
Aliovalent 3+ dopants (for example In3+) introduce lithium vacancies via charge compensation in Li2−yM1±xCl4 spinel solid electrolytes (i.e., an In3+-driven vacancy mechanism).
In Li2−yM1±xCl4 chloride spinel compositions the total positive charge from the cations must balance the four chloride anions (sum of cation charges = +4 for Cl4) to satisfy charge neutrality.

In this dataset, multi-2+ cation mixing (e.g., Mn/Fe/Mg/Cu) correlates with maintenance of a disordered Fd-3m spinel framework and with improved ionic conductivity relative to less mixed compositions.
The dataset shows Li1.8Mn1.1Cl4 (x = +0.1, all 2+) achieves an ionic conductivity of 1.75e-05 S/cm.
In this dataset, the Li1.8Mn1.1Cl4 (x = +0.1, all 2+) composition avoids Li3MCl6-type side phases that appear when Y3+ and In3+ are present.
In this dataset, Li3MCl6-type competing frameworks are observed with Y3+ and In3+ dopants.
Within this dataset, several aliovalently doped samples exhibit ordering tendencies that correlate with lower ionic conductivity.
Some Mg-containing samples in the dataset require higher synthesis temperatures (≈450 °C) to realize their best ionic conductivity.

Metal-excess (x > 0) compositions containing only divalent cations can produce lithium vacancies and thereby achieve appreciable ionic conductivity without introducing 3+/4+/5+ dopants (this mechanism is the rationale given for the observed metal-excess compositions).
Using metal excess of approximately x ≈ +0.2 is intended to introduce vacancies via metal excess, analogous to the Mn-only x = +0.1 case that performed well in the dataset.
A broad trend reported in this campaign is that multication spinels reach ionic conductivities in the 10^-5–10^-4 S/cm range when the spinel network is preserved.
High cation configurational disorder on the 16d site is generally favorable for frustrating Li/M ordering and lowering Li-ion migration barriers.
Divalent-only, high-entropy cation mixes (Fe/Ni/Co/Cu/Mg) avoid the Y/In-associated Li3MCl6-type side phases observed in the dataset with trivalent dopants.
In this dataset, Ta5+ ≈ 0.2 reliably delivers high ionic conductivity when ordering is suppressed; for example, Li1.4Fe0.8Ta0.2Cl4 exhibited an ionic conductivity of 2.35e-05 S/cm at 450 °C.
In this dataset, Mn2+ co-doping mitigates Nb/Ta-driven ordering and recovers ionic conductivity; for example, Li1.4Fe0.7Mn0.1Nb0.2Cl4 showed ionic conductivity in the range 1.17e-05–2.03e-05 S/cm.

In this dataset, Sn2+ appears compatible with vacancy-rich, disordered spinels that give high ionic conductivity; for example, Li1.7Fe0.62Sn0.2Ta0.06Y0.12Cl4 exhibited an ionic conductivity of 3.64e-05 S/cm.

In this dataset, multi-cation, vacancy-rich compositions can still be single-phase and exhibit high ionic conductivity; for example, Li1.5Fe0.3Nb0.1Mn0.1In0.2Mg0.3Cl4 showed an ionic conductivity of 2.36e-05 S/cm.
Within this dataset's uncertainty assessment, heavy Mg content and very low Li content increase the risk of LiCl exsolution and/or Cmmm-type ordering.

In this dataset, Mn+Zr co-doping is a strong performer: the composition Li1.4Fe0.7Mn0.3Zr0.1Cl4 exhibited ionic conductivities of 3.31e-05 S/cm when synthesized at 400 °C and 5.35e-05 S/cm when synthesized at 500 °C.

In this dataset, Ta5+ substitution was observed to introduce vacancies and can deliver high ionic conductivity when cation ordering is suppressed; for example Li1.4Fe0.8Ta0.2Cl4 showed an ionic conductivity of 2.35e-05 S/cm at 450 °C.

In this dataset, Co2+ was found to be acceptable in small amounts provided cation disorder is high, and observed ionic conductivity increased with higher synthesis temperature or with reduced Co content.
In this dataset, Nb- or Ta-only spinel compositions with approximately 0.2 Nb/Ta content were observed to be more prone to cation ordering (i.e., more ordering-prone) than lower Nb/Ta levels.
In this dataset, higher Co content was associated with problematic spinel formation at 400 °C (spinel formation became problematic above certain Co levels at that temperature).
A low-angle X-ray diffraction feature near ~15° 2θ is a known ordering signature in these chloride spinel materials.
In this dataset, Mn addition suppressed the low-angle ~15° 2θ ordering feature in Nb/Ta-containing analogue compositions.
An abnormally high ionic conductivity (σ) was observed at 450 °C for the composition Li1.6Ni0.4V0.4Zn0.2Cl4 in this study.
For Li1.6Ni0.4V0.4Zn0.2Cl4, Zn2+-driven cation-site disorder is kinetically stabilized at 450 °C but relaxes toward a more ordered, lower-mobility configuration at 500 °C.
In spinel frameworks, greater Li/M cation disorder combined with a well-connected lithium-vacancy network reduces Li-ion migration barriers.
Zn2+ commonly favors tetrahedral coordination in spinel families, biasing the cation distribution in ways that can enhance Li/M disorder.

At fixed y = 0.4 (Ni+Zn = 0.6, V = 0.4), increasing Zn content is expected to further strengthen the disordered, high-mobility state at 450 °C and to raise room-temperature ionic conductivity (σRT), provided the spinel framework remains the dominant phase.

At 450 °C, Li1.6Ni0.4V0.4Zn0.2Cl4 exhibits room-temperature ionic conductivity σRT = 2.5e-06 S/cm and XRD indicates a majority spinel phase (Fd-3m, fraction 0.8461) with a NiCl2 impurity (fraction 0.1539).
At 450 °C, Li1.6Ni0.6V0.4Cl4 (Zn removed, y ≈ 0.4) exhibits σRT = 2.26e-07 S/cm and is majority spinel by XRD (spinel fraction 0.9043).

Within this dataset, comparison of the two 450 °C samples (Li1.6Ni0.4V0.4Zn0.2Cl4 vs Li1.6Ni0.6V0.4Cl4) shows a correlation between the presence of Zn and substantially higher σRT under otherwise similar synthesis conditions.
Li1.6Ni0.4V0.4Zn0.2Cl4 synthesized at 500 °C is single-phase spinel by XRD but has σRT = 1.55e-07 S/cm, which is much lower than the 450 °C sample of the same composition.

The observed drop in σRT for the Zn-containing composition between 450 °C and 500 °C in this dataset indicates that the high-conductivity state present at 450 °C is not retained after higher-temperature annealing, a behavior consistent with cation/vacancy ordering upon higher-T anneal.
Multiple Ni-based analogues synthesized at 500 °C using various doping strategies (Sc3+/Y3+/Zr4++V3+/Ta5++V3+) show σRT on the order of 1e-08–1e-07 S/cm with spinel indexing in XRD.
Within this dataset, Ni-host spinel compositions synthesized at 500 °C are typically low in σRT unless the specific Zn-containing, 450 °C condition is met.
In spinel frameworks, Li+ transport is improved by Li/M site disorder and by the presence of percolating Li-vacancy networks (general crystallographic/transport principle).

Zn2+ commonly prefers tetrahedral coordination in spinel families, which can bias cation distributions and thereby promote Li/M disorder that lowers Li+ migration barriers (general crystallographic knowledge).
X-ray diffraction cannot directly resolve Li/M site disorder in spinel structures, so ionic transport measurements (conductivity) can serve as a sensitive proxy for detecting such disorder.

X-ray diffraction (Rietveld) refinement for the Ni-based inverse-spinel sample indicates a majority spinel phase (space group Fd-3m) fraction = 0.8461, a NiCl2 impurity fraction = 0.1539, and Rwp = 6.85%.
The room-temperature ionic conductivity of the Ni-based inverse-spinel sample is 2.5e-06 S/cm.

The 2.5e-06 S/cm conductivity is an order of magnitude or more higher than measured conductivities of multiple Ni-based compositions synthesized at 450–500 °C: Li1.6Ni0.6V0.4Cl4 (2.26e-07 S/cm), Li1.4Ni1.0V0.2Cl4 (2.1e-08 S/cm), Li1.8Ni0.8Y0.2Cl4 (4.82e-08 S/cm), Li1.70Ni0.80Zr0.10V0.10Cl4 (5.7e-08 S/cm), and Li1.60Ni0.80V0.10Ta0.10Cl4 (6.07e-08 S/cm).
The vacancy-doped Ni-spinel composition Li1.75Ni0.75Sc0.25Cl4 measured a conductivity of 9.15e-07 S/cm in this dataset.
A same-composition/high-temperature check for Li1.6Ni0.4V0.4Zn0.2Cl4 synthesized at 500 °C showed a conductivity of 1.55e-07 S/cm.
Compared to the 500 °C check and other Ni-based samples in this dataset, the 2.5e-06 S/cm measurement at 450 °C is an outlier within the Ni-host spinel set.
Given the dominant spinel fraction in the refinement and no identified high-conductivity secondary phase, the measured 2.5e-06 S/cm value is abnormally high for Ni-host spinels in this dataset.
Li1.5Mg0.5In0.5Cl4 exhibits an abnormally high room-temperature ionic conductivity (σRT) relative to spinel-only baseline compositions in this experimental campaign.
The Li1.5Mg0.5In0.5Cl4 sample in this study was synthesized at a lower temperature of 400 °C.
The Li1.5Mg0.5In0.5Cl4 composition contains heterovalent In3+ substitution on the M sublattice.
The Li1.5Mg0.5In0.5Cl4 sample exhibits a high degree of Li/M sublattice disorder and Li-vacancy disorder.
In Li1.5Mg0.5In0.5Cl4, the Li/M sublattice and Li-vacancy disorder expand the three-dimensional Li+ percolation network and lower Li-ion migration barriers.
The average spinel arrangement is described by the space group Fd-3m (the 'average Fd-3m arrangement').
A reduction in the number of unindexed peaks in powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns indicates convergence toward the average Fd-3m spinel arrangement.

A Li stoichiometry of Li1.5 in Li2−yM1Cl4 corresponds to approximately y ≈ 0.5 lithium vacancies when the average metal (M) valence is +2.5 (for example, 0.5 Mn2+ + 0.5 M3+).
High Li-vacancy content generally increases ionic conductivity in spinel materials (basic defect-transport principle).

Despite the high Li-vacancy content implied by Li1.5 stoichiometry, Li1.5Mn0.5Y0.5Cl4 synthesized at 450 °C in this dataset exhibits low room-temperature conductivity and contains substantial Li3YCl6, indicating that vacancy content alone did not yield high conductivity in this case.

At 400 °C the mixed Y/In sample (Li1.5Mn0.5Y0.25In0.25Cl4) shows a spinel-only refinement and the highest room-temperature σ among the tested Y-containing samples at that temperature, whereas Y-only compositions at 400 °C show measurable Li3YCl6 (for example, Li1.8Mn0.8Y0.2Cl4 with 0.1292 weight fraction Li3YCl6).

In this dataset, mixed Y/In co-doping correlates with suppression of Li3YCl6 formation near 400 °C and with realization of a more disordered, vacancy-rich spinel exhibiting higher ionic conductivity compared to Y-only compositions.

A synthesis temperature of 400 °C lies within the successful thermal window for halide spinels in this dataset and is the temperature at which the anomalously high room-temperature σ was observed for the Y/In sample.

In this dataset, increasing the synthesis temperature to 450 °C alters the secondary phase (observed to change to Li3YCl6) and/or reduces favorable boundary connectivity in the microstructure, and this change is associated with a lowered room-temperature ionic conductivity (σRT) for the same composition.

Across the reported samples, the observed pattern—higher macroscopic conductivity when an In-containing Li–halide secondary phase is present at 400 °C, and lower conductivity when the secondary phase is Y-rich (or when compositions contain no In)—is consistent with an added contribution from an In-containing Li–halide secondary phase boosting pellet-scale conductivity beyond a spinel-only baseline in this experimental campaign.
